Fundamentals — the resource-control core

Leader philosophy

BY Nami is a resource-control midrange that wins by out-economizing the opponent, not out-statting them. Across 714 ranked games in the CDN window — the unbiased aggregate of every ranked match, not upload-filtered replays — she holds 52.0% at 11.2% presence, and the spread around that average is enormous: her worst meta pairing sits at 28.1% over 96 games while her best runs 64.9% over 77. That polarity is the signature of an engine deck: where the opponent can't punish the engine, the engine buries them. The skill ceiling is just as loud — all ten of the top tracked pilots sit at 73.5% or better, led by haru#6484 at 19W-3L (86.4%) with a median Elo floor of 2421. This deck pays you for reps.

The leader text is two separate economies. The [Your Turn] draw converts every life movement on your turn — yours or theirs — into a card: 13,836 recorded activations across the 42,760-line sim corpus. The [DON!! x1] buff converts any card in hand into +2000 leader power on defense, once per opposing turn. Together: Nami draws more cards than she has any right to, then spends the surplus to make a 5000 leader defend like a 7000 one. Neither effect wins alone — the draw keeps the buff funded, the buff keeps your real counters and life intact, and intact life is fuel for the next round of draws.

Four life is the printed number, not the real one. Nico Robin trashes one of your life cards to stack two back — net +1, and the trash itself fires the leader draw because it happens on your turn. Marshall D. Teach banks a chosen card face-down on top of life. Roronoa Zoro turns a spare hand card into a life card. Borsalino refills when you're at 2 or less. Zeus and Kouzuki Hiyori withdraw life into hand on demand, paying you a draw on the way out. Life is a checking account: every deposit can hide a Trigger, and every your-turn withdrawal is a card.

The third hand is the trash. The buff's observed fodder is not garbage: Kikunojo (1,709 trashes), Edward.Newgate (1,605), Gecko Moria (1,395), Dr. Hogback (1,329), Perona (1,297), Nico Robin (1,247). Hogback and Perona aren't being discarded, they're being staged — Gecko Moria plays a 4-cost Thriller Bark body straight from trash or stacks it face-up onto your life, and the Kumacy / Dr. Hogback / Perona Triggers do the same. Trashing a card to strip 2000 power off an attack, then replaying that same card later, is the deck's defining exchange.

Here is this chapter's thesis, straight from the replay corpus (seven tracked opposing decks, two seat splits each — 14 won-game and 14 lost-game samples per turn): the early game does not separate winners from losers; late-game solvency does. On T2-T3 the take, counter, and buff rates of won and lost games are nearly identical, and both sit at median 4 life. The fork opens at T5-T6: winners hold 3+ life in 9 of 14 T6 splits while losers sit at 2 or less in 11 of 14. By T8 the gap is brutal — every won split still countered at least 31% of defenses (no lost split cleared 35%), 10 of 14 won splits still paid the +2000 over 70% of the time (versus 3 of 14 lost), and nine lost splits took more raw damage than the tankiest won split. Losers didn't choose worse defenses on T8; they arrived broke. Everything below — life, hand, DON — is about arriving at T6-T8 solvent.

Seat choice compounds all of it: Nami wins 56.4% on the draw against 51.0% on the play, in a sim field whose baseline already tilts 52.6/47.4 the same direction. She beats par from both chairs, but her even-cost spine — 2-cost engine starters into 8-cost bombs — is happiest with the second player's DON track. Take second on the roll, with exactly one exception covered in the turn-order section: the mirror.

Life-Removal Draw Engine
“[Your Turn] [Once Per Turn] This effect can be activated when a card is removed from your or your opponent's Life cards. If you have 7 or less cards in your hand, draw 1 card.”

This is a [Your Turn] effect — read that twice, because it defines the deck's tempo. Damage you take on the opponent's turn draws you nothing; it only banks Trigger equity. The draw fires when a life card is removed on YOUR turn, from either side: your attacks connecting with their life, Nami (053) lifting the top card of their life into their hand, Nico Robin trashing the top of your own life, Zeus or Kouzuki Hiyori moving your life into your hand. Cards ADDED to life (Marshall D. Teach, Roronoa Zoro) do not qualify, and neither does Nico Robin's On K.O. burn, because that resolves on the opponent's turn. Two operational rules fall out of the once-per-turn and hand-size clauses. First, only the first qualifying removal each turn pays — a triple-attack turn draws one card, not three, which also means a quiet development turn with Zeus banks the exact same draw. Second, the check is hand at 7 or less when you activate it: sitting at 8 cards, deploy first and attack second, or the draw fizzles.

13,836 leader-draw activations are recorded across the 42,760-line sim corpus — this fires in essentially every game, repeatedly. The cheapest igniters also carry the best opener numbers: hands containing Nami (053) won 57.5% on the play (n=162) and 64.4% on the draw (n=141); Girl openers won 58.5% / 58.8% (n=53/55); Zeus openers 55.7% / 57.7% (n=189/70). Correlation, not causation — but it's the engine package leading the keep table, not the bombs.

+2000 Defensive Buff
“[DON!! x1] [On Your Opponent's Attack] [Once Per Turn] You may trash 1 card from your hand: This Leader gains +2000 power during this turn.”

On defense Nami is a 5000 leader with a once-per-turn toll booth. With at least one DON attached — rested counts, which is why Nami (053), Girl and Edward.Newgate all shovel rested DON onto her — any card in your hand becomes +2000: 5000 + 2000 = 7000, so an unsupported 6000 swing simply fails, while a 7000 swing still connects because the attacker wins ties. The wording 'gains +2000 power during this turn' means the buff is not per-attack: fire it on their first leader attack and every later swing that turn also runs into 7000. The strategic weight is counter economy — 8 of the 20 consensus staples print no counter value at all, and this effect is how those cards defend. The price is the resource trio in miniature: 1 DON parked on the leader, 1 card paid from hand, every single turn. Budget for it.

Usage is near-universal early — 12 of 14 won-game replay splits buffed between 54% and 86% of tracked T2 defenses while 8 of those splits countered under 10% — and persistence is what separates records: on T8, 10 of 14 won splits still activated the buff over 70% of the time versus 3 of 14 lost splits (lost-split floor: 48.2%). The fodder counts confirm what it eats: Kikunojo 1,709 trashes, Edward.Newgate 1,605, Gecko Moria 1,395, Dr. Hogback 1,329, Perona 1,297, Nico Robin 1,247 — counterless cards and recyclable Thriller Bark bodies. No 2000-counter card makes the top-fodder list, and that's not an accident.

❤️ LIFE — your fourth resource

Life is the deck's most liquid currency, and the data says winners spend it early and hoard it late. On T2, won-game replay splits show counter rates under 10% in 8 of 14 samples (as low as 2.4%) with take rates running to 91.5% in one split — winners let early hits through, bank the Triggers, and still sit at median 4 life through T3 in 8 of 14 splits. Early damage is cheap because the refill package puts it back. Nico Robin is the headline: trash the top of your life, stack two from deck — net +1 life, and because the trash happens on your turn it fires the leader draw too. Marshall D. Teach adds a chosen card face-down from your top 3. Roronoa Zoro converts a spare hand card into a life card. Borsalino adds one when you're at 2 or less. Gecko Moria can even stack a Thriller Bark body from your trash face-up onto life — a known card you can plan around.

⚠️ damage on the opponent's turn draws you nothing — the leader draw is [Your Turn] only. Life you take is Trigger equity and saved counters, not cards. Life you SPEND on your own turn is double-paid: Zeus or Kouzuki Hiyori moves a life card into your hand (+1 card) and fires the leader draw on the way (+1 more), turning one point of life into two cards plus an effect.

The medians draw the map. Winners and losers both hold median 4 life through T3. The first median-2 samples appear in lost splits on T4; no won split drops below 3 until T5, and only one sits there. At T6 winners hold 3 or better in 9 of 14 splits while losers are at 2 or less in 11 of 14 — that one-life gap is the game. By T8 won splits sit at 2 in 12 of 14 (two still at 3); five of 14 lost splits are already at 1.

🎯 cross into T6 at 3 life. Below that, every swing is lethal-range, the +2000 stops covering the math alone, and Borsalino is your only road back. Treat life like a loan with repayment already arranged — Nico Robin in hand is permission to tank; no refill in sight means tightening up a full turn earlier than feels natural.

✋ HAND — fuel and shield

Hand is the ammunition and the thermostat — the leader draw refills it, the buff and counters drain it, and 7 is the magic number. The draw checks '7 or less cards' at activation: at 8+ your engine is off. Sequence accordingly — when you untap with a fat hand, deploy and pay costs BEFORE the first life-removing action of the turn, so the draw is live when it matters.

Counter economy is the deck's quiet constraint. Eight of the 20 consensus staples print no counter at all (Nico Robin, Edward.Newgate, Gecko Moria, Marshall D. Teach, Roronoa Zoro, Marco, Kikunojo, Gravity Blade Raging Tiger), and only four print 2000 (Zeus, Kumacy, Baby 5, Kouzuki Hiyori). Raw counter density is thin by design — the +2000 buff is the equalizer that lets a counterless card defend the leader for 2000's worth. That makes every trash decision a ranked hierarchy, and the corpus shows exactly what good pilots feed it:

1. Free fodder — surplus Edward.Newgate (1,605 observed trashes), Kikunojo (1,709), extra Nico Robin copies (1,247): no counter stat lost, no recursion lost. 2. Deposits — Dr. Hogback (1,329) and Perona (1,297): they carry 1000 counter, but trashing them is storage, not loss — Gecko Moria plays them back from trash, and the Kumacy / Dr. Hogback / Perona Triggers do the same. 3. Never — the 2000-counters and the counters you've earmarked for their endgame swings. No 2000-counter card appears in the observed top-fodder list.

Filtering keeps the engine fed without breaching the cap: Girl draws 1 and trashes 1 on play, Edward.Newgate draws 2 and trashes 1 while arming the leader with DON, and Mr. 3 cashes himself in for 2 cards plus an attack lock.

🗝️ the losing pattern in this corpus is hand bankruptcy, and you can see it in the buff line — on T8, 10 of 14 won splits still paid the +2000 over 70% of the time against 3 of 14 lost splits, with the lost rate flooring at 48.2%. Losers didn't decide to stop defending; the fodder ran out. Run the audit every turn from T5: if you can't afford one buff card plus one real counter per turn through T8, you overspent somewhere around T4.

💠 DON!! — the tempo dial

Nami's DON rule: the leader is never naked on defense. The buff reads [DON!! x1] — at least one DON attached when they attack — and rested DON satisfies it. The deck is built to meet the requirement for free: Nami (053) gives a rested DON to the leader on play, Edward.Newgate gives the leader up to 2 rested DON on top of drawing you cards, and Girl's Activate Main hands a rested DON to a [Nami] card once per turn — your leader is a [Nami] card. So the attach pattern each turn is: spend the whole pool on deployment and attacks, then re-arm the leader with rested DON through those effects. No attacher available? Put one DON on the leader manually before you swing — it buys +1000 on offense (5000 + 1000 = 6000) and stays attached through their turn to keep the buff legal. The only strictly wrong line is ending your turn with zero DON on her while holding a hand full of fodder you now can't spend.

On curve, the spine is even-costed: Zeus / Girl / Kouzuki Hiyori at 2, Perona / Dr. Hogback / Roronoa Zoro / Marco at 4, Gecko Moria and Marshall D. Teach at 8 — with Nami (053) at 5, Nico Robin at 7, and Edward.Newgate at 10 as the odd-cost flex. Going second's even DON totals (2-4-6-8-10) land all of it on schedule and reach the 8-drops a full turn cycle before the first player — part of why the seat split reads 56.4% second versus 51.0% first across 714 CDN games. Going first, Nami (053) on exactly 5 DON and Nico Robin on exactly 7 keep the curve honest but leave no spare DON, which makes the free attachers load-bearing.

Defense math — take, counter, or buff?

Every incoming attack asks one question: what is the cheapest way to make this fail — or is failing fine? The menu, priced:

  • Take it (0 cards). No draw — it's their turn — but real Trigger equity: the recursion package (Kumacy, Dr. Hogback, Perona, Gecko Moria, Kikunojo, Baby 5, Marshall D. Teach) all carry Triggers, several of which put a free body in play or draw 2.
  • Buff (1 card — ANY card). 5000 base + 2000 = 7000: their 6000 swing now fails outright; a 7000 swing still connects because the attacker wins ties. Once per turn, and it lasts the whole turn — fired on their first attack, it covers every attack after it.
  • Counter from hand. A 1000 counter alone = 6000: stops only 5000. Buff + 1000 counter = 8000: blanks 7000. Buff + 2000 = 9000: blanks 8000. Countering without the buff underneath is a bad exchange rate in a deck with only four 2000-counter staples.
  • Block. Marco is the premier profit-block: a 6000 blocker that draws 2 when KO'd. Borsalino blocks at 6000 and refills life when you're at 2 or less. Edward.Newgate is a 12000 wall. Sanji is the budget 4000 body.

The replay corpus turns that menu into a schedule.

T2-T3 — buff or take, never counter. 12 of 14 won splits buffed 54-86% of tracked T2 defenses; 8 of 14 countered under 10% (low: 2.4%); take rates in won splits ran as high as 91.5%. At 4 life with refills in the deck, early damage is the cheapest item on the menu.

T4-T5 — the pivot. Counter rates in won splits climb: 10 of 14 T5 won splits countered 32% or more, with the mirror splits topping the table at 50.4% and 49.5%, while median life slides from 4 to 3. Their swings now arrive at 7000+, the buff alone stops covering the math, and buff-plus-1000 (8000) becomes the standard receipt.

T6-T8 — full price discipline. Winners hold all three rates at once. At T8, every won split countered at least 31% of defenses and no lost split cleared 35%; 10 of 14 won splits kept the buff above 70% against 3 of 14 lost; the tankiest won split took 46.0% of attacks while nine lost splits took more than that. In the won mirror splits at T6, players buffed 83.4% / 86.3% of tracked defenses and took only 24.9% / 19.4%, against 34.4% / 32.7% taken in the lost splits — same matchup, same tools, one life of difference in outcome.

⚠️ the late-game numbers are not advice you can apply on T8 — they are the audit of your T2-T5 spending. If T7-you cannot pay one fodder card plus one counter per turn, T4-you bought something you didn't need.

Mulligan guide

The first lesson of the keep table: there are no auto-keeps in this deck. Keep rates cluster between 35% and 53% on nearly every card — the field keeps hands, not cards — and the lone outlier is telling: Gravity Blade Raging Tiger at 62.8% on the play (n=43), the one card that answers boards Nami can't fight through. What you're actually assembling is the engine-starter package. The three best WR-in-hand cards at scale are Nami (053) (57.5% first / 64.4% second), Girl (58.5% / 58.8%) and Zeus (55.7% / 57.7%) — the cheap life-touchers that switch the leader draw on by T2-T3. Note that Nami (053)'s steal clause requires the opponent at 3 or more life: she is an opening-hand card by design and gets worse every turn their life drops.

Seat shifts are real. Going second the field holds the defensive bridge: Marco keep jumps from 42.9% to 58.8%, Girl from 37.7% to 52.7%, Baby 5 from 42.5% to 51.4%, Marshall D. Teach from 44.4% to 52.6%. Going first the proactive plan rules: Nami (053) is kept 48.8% on the play but only 34.0% on the draw — and that second number looks like the table's biggest leak, because second-seat openers containing her won 64.4% (n=141), the best large-sample cell in the dataset (the two cells above it, Silvers Rayleigh and Gravity Blade Raging Tiger second seat, sit on n=10 apiece). Correlation isn't causation, but when keep behavior and outcomes point opposite directions, side with the outcomes.

The reverse trap also shows up: Borsalino is in 98.3% of lists, yet openers holding him underperform (42.9% / 44.7%) — a staple you play from the deck's flow, not a keep criterion. Same for Kumacy at 35.4% WR-in-hand on the play (n=199), the worst large-sample cell: he's a Trigger, and a Trigger in your opening hand is a Trigger that isn't in your life.

⚠️ rows under n=30 (Kingdom Come, Sanji and Nico Robin (109) both seats; Silvers Rayleigh, Kouzuki Hiyori, Gravity Blade Raging Tiger and Kikunojo second seat) are directional at best — read the note column before trusting them.

First or second?

Take second. The CDN numbers are unambiguous: 56.4% on the draw versus 51.0% on the play across the 714-game window, in a sim field whose overall baseline already tilts second 52.6 to 47.4. Nami beats par from both chairs, and the curve explains the lean: the spine is even-costed — 2-cost engine starters, 4-cost Thriller Bark bodies, 8-cost Gecko Moria and Marshall D. Teach — and the second player's DON track (2-4-6-8) deploys all of it on schedule, reaching the 8-drops a full turn cycle earlier with spare DON left over for leader attachment on the 5- and 7-cost turns. Going first buys tempo instead: Nami (053) on exactly 5 DON starts stealing while their life is guaranteed full, but Nico Robin on exactly 7 and the 8-drops waiting until 9 DON leave the curve a half-step late all game.

The biggest seat flip in the data is the mirror: Nami versus Nami ran 64.3% for the first player and 35.7% for the second (n=34 — thin, but a 29-point spread). Three other CDN cells lean first by smaller margins — Enel (OP15-058) at 50.0 first / 42.9 second (n=38), Sengoku at 66.7 / 46.2 (n=24), Donquixote Rosinante (061) at 60.9 / 59.1 (n=58) — but those gaps sit inside sub-sample noise; the mirror is the only flip large and clean enough to act on. The mechanical story is easy to rationalize: both leaders feed on life removal, so the player who attacks first switches their draw engine on first and keeps their own life intact longer against the opponent's steal-clause checks — in a compounding engine, earlier is everything. Treat the magnitude with small-sample skepticism, but if you win the roll into the mirror, play first; in every other pairing, draw.

Universal tips

  1. Deploy before you attack whenever your hand sits at 8: the leader draw checks '7 or less' at the moment it activates, and only the first life removal each turn pays out.

  2. Damage you take never draws you a card — the draw is [Your Turn] only. Take hits for Trigger equity and saved resources, not card flow.

  3. Default early defense is buff-or-take: in 8 of 14 won-game replay splits, T2 counter rates were under 10%. Your counters are mid- and late-game cards.

  4. Fire the +2000 on their first real attack of the turn — 'during this turn' means every later swing that turn also runs into 7000.

  5. Feed the buff in order: surplus Edward.Newgate / Kikunojo / Nico Robin first (1,605 / 1,709 / 1,247 observed trashes), then Dr. Hogback and Perona as deposits Gecko Moria can withdraw. No 2000-counter card makes the observed fodder list — keep it that way.

  6. Never end your turn with a DON-less leader. Nami (053), Girl and Edward.Newgate attach rested DON for free, and rested DON fully satisfies the [DON!! x1] requirement on defense.

  7. No profitable attack? The engine still runs: Zeus or Kouzuki Hiyori on a quiet turn converts one life card into hand plus the leader draw.

  8. 🎯 enter T6 at 3 life. Winners held 3 or better in 9 of 14 replay splits; losers sat at 2 or less in 11 of 14. Nico Robin in hand is your license to tank early.

  9. Late counters are the winning signature: by T8 every won split countered at least 31% of defenses and no lost split cleared 35%. Budget two defensive cards per turn from T6 on — one fodder, one real counter.

  10. Audit your take rate: the tankiest won split took 46% of T8 attacks and nine of 14 lost splits took more. If you're face-tanking T7-T8 because the hand is empty, the loss actually happened on T4.

  11. Choose second on the roll (56.4% vs 51.0% across 714 CDN games) — except the mirror, where first ran 64.3% (n=34, thin but lopsided).

  12. Going second, keep Nami (053) openers: the field ships her back 66% of the time, yet hands containing her won 64.4% of those games (n=141).

  13. Marco is a planned casualty — block the biggest swing, die, draw 2. A two-for-one you chose the timing on.

  14. Zeus has three jobs: KO a 5-cost-or-less on play, life-to-hand engine fuel, and one of only four 2000-counter staples. Decide which job each copy has before you spend it.

Decklist & card options

What this deck is. BY Nami is OP16's resource-control midrange: a 4-life, 5000-power leader who converts every life-card movement into a drawn card and every spare card in hand into +2000 of defense, until Edward Newgate and Gecko Moria end the game at 10000-12000 a swing.

Read the leader text as two separate machines. The draw half — [Your Turn], once per turn, hand at 7 or less — fires whenever a card leaves either player's life pile on your turn. Your attacks cracking their life do it, but so do your own effects: Nami (053) pulls the top of the opponent's life into their hand, Zeus and Kouzuki Hiyori bank your own life into hand, Nico Robin trashes one of your life cards to restack two. The deck is built so the trigger has fuel even on turns your attacks don't connect: the corpus logged 13,836 leader draws across 42,760 sim log lines. That loop — not any single card — is the deck's card advantage.

The defense half — 1 DON on the leader, trash 1 card from hand, once per turn — turns any card into a 2000-counter: 5000 base + 2000 = 7000, so every 6000 swing on the ladder fails into her. It stacks with attached DON, which persists through the opponent's turn (given DON only returns at your refresh phase): the rested DON Nami (053) or Girl banks on her makes it 8000, and the two from Edward Newgate make it 9000. The logs show players feed the trash cost exactly what theory predicts — counterless cards first: Kikunojo (1,709 pitches), spare Edward Newgate copies (1,605), Gecko Moria (1,395), then Dr. Hogback (1,329) and Perona (1,297), whose 1000 counters are worth less from hand than the +2000 they buy when trashed.

The third pillar is life as a curated zone, not a hit-point bar. The Thriller Bark package makes every life card the opponent cracks a lottery against them: Kumacy's trigger fired 1,390 times in the corpus — the highest count in the deck — with Gecko Moria at 1,264, Perona at 1,034, and Dr. Hogback at 1,002. And the deck keeps restocking the pile mid-game: Gecko Moria, Marshall D. Teach, Roronoa Zoro, and Kouzuki Hiyori all add cards to life, several of them chosen or face-up.

🎯 out-resource, then out-size. Every life you take draws you a card, every life they take risks a trigger, and your hand never empties because the leader and Edward Newgate keep refilling it. Across 3,191 pooled ranked games the consensus locks roughly 46 of 50 main-deck slots — what follows is a solved core plus a four-slot argument, and the highest-WR pilots all take the same side of it.

Card-by-card

Nami

The leader is the deck's engine and its best defensive card. Her recorded swings cluster at 6000-8000 — about 81% of roughly 19,500 logged leader attacks, modal 7000 — which is base 5000 plus the 1-3 DON the deck banks on her via Nami (053), Girl, and Edward Newgate rather than spending them. 🗝️ the draw fires only on your turn and only at hand 7 or less, so the life-manipulation suite exists to guarantee the trigger even on turns your attacks don't connect — 13,836 leader draws in the corpus. On defense, leave at least 1 DON attached when you pass; trashing any card then lifts her to 5000 + 2000 = 7000 against one attack per turn. The logs show the trash priority is counterless cards first (Kikunojo 1,709 pitches, spare Edward Newgate 1,605), then 1000-counter bodies — pitching Dr. Hogback for +2000 beats countering with him for +1000 whenever the buff alone repels the attack.

Nami (053)

The defining tempo play and the most curve-locked card in the list: 2,045 of her 2,673 recorded deploys — over three-quarters — land on turn 3, on either side of the coin flip. Five DON buys a 6000 body, a rested DON moved to the leader (she swings 1000 higher that turn and, because attached DON persists through the opponent's turn, defends at 6000 — 8000 with the buff), and the top card of the opponent's life moved to their hand while they still have 3+ life: that fires your leader draw and deletes a future Trigger window without dealing combat damage. The On K.O. clause — turn your top life face-up to deploy a 6000-power-or-less character from hand — taxes removal on the way out. She is also real defensive stock: 2,284 recorded 1000-counter uses. Always 4; play her on curve.

Nico Robin (055)

The life restacker: 71% of her 3,647 deploys come on turns 4-5. The On Play line — trash your top life card, then stack the top 2 cards of your deck onto life — is net +1 life, fires the leader draw (a card left your life on your turn), and leaves an 8000 Strike body that swung at exactly 8000 in about two-thirds of her roughly 4,900 recorded attacks. The [Opponent's Turn] [On K.O.] clause — deal 1 damage to the opponent — means removing her in battle costs them a life card, so she usually just gets ignored and keeps swinging. No counter, so spare copies become buff fodder: she is the #6 trash in the corpus at 1,247 pitches. Always 4.

Zeus (SP)

The deck's premier defensive card in observed practice: 5,360 recorded 2000-counter uses — the highest counter count in the deck — against roughly 1,480 deploys, meaning he is countered three to four times as often as he is played. When you do board him (deploys spread evenly across turns 2-7), he converts your own top-or-bottom life card into a hand card — firing the leader draw and turning an unknown life card into guaranteed resources — to K.O. a cost-5-or-less character: removal stapled to the engine. ⚠️ playing him drops your life count by one; against decks with burn or reach, count whether the K.O. is worth the life point. Always 4 — but the default job is 2000 counter.

Borsalino

Borsalino is the mid-game wall: about 74% of his roughly 4,720 deploys land on turns 5-8, exactly the window where Nami lists stabilize. A 6000 [Blocker] whose On Play refunds a life card from the top of your deck when you are at 2 or less — the state this deck reaches on purpose after trading early life for leader draws. He also logged 2,236 recorded 1000-counter uses, so late copies are never dead. The body math matters: a 6000 blocker forces 7000+ from attackers, which taxes DON the opponent wanted for development. Always 4.

Edward.Newgate (SP)

The stabilizer-finisher: 85% of 3,597 deploys land turns 5-7. The split is the curve telling on itself — the 844 turn-5 deploys are going-second games, where 10 DON arrives a turn earlier, while turn 6 (1,484, the modal turn) is the going-first slot. On play: draw 2, trash 1 — hand sculpting that feeds the buff — then give up to 2 rested DON each to the leader and a character. Those DON persist through the opponent's turn, so the leader defends at 5000 + 2000 attached = 7000 passively and 9000 with the trash buff — at 9000, almost nothing on the ladder connects without dumping multiple counters. As a 12000 [Blocker] he swung at exactly 12000 in about 71% of his 2,809 recorded attacks and blanks most leader swings permanently. He is also the #2 buff-trash at 1,605 pitches. 3 is the number: the 10-DON turn comes once or twice, and extra copies are 2000-counters via the leader.

Gecko Moria

Gecko Moria is the Thriller Bark payoff: about 74% of roughly 2,450 deploys land turns 4-6 — turn 4 (451 deploys) is the going-second 8-DON curve, turn 5 (917, modal) the going-first one. On play he reanimates a cost-4-or-less Thriller Bark body from trash — a free Perona freeze or Dr. Hogback K.O.-shield — or stacks it face-up onto your life, converting a known trigger into guaranteed value when that life cracks. His own trigger (play any cost-4-or-less from trash) fired 1,264 times, second-highest in the deck. The body is a 10000 that swung at exactly 10000 in 70% of his 2,847 recorded attacks. No counter, so he doubles as the #3 buff-trash at 1,395 pitches. Always 4: fuel, payoff, and beater in one card.

Perona

Perona is three cards in one slot. As a deploy (modal turns 2-4: 101, 194, and 172 recorded deploys) she shuts a cost-6-or-less attacker off for the opponent's next turn — and the same effect repeats On K.O., so removing her re-triggers it. As defense she logged 2,258 recorded 1000-counter uses against about 770 deploys — countered roughly three times as often as played — and she is the #5 buff-trash at 1,297 pitches, where her card converts to +2000 instead of +1000. Her trigger fired 1,034 times. When she does attack, over half her recorded swings are naked 5000s — cheap pressure into rested boards that forces counters or trades up via the freeze. Always 4; board her only when the freeze buys a full turn.

Kumacy

Never board this card. The corpus shows about ten recorded deploys ever — against 4,662 recorded 2000-counter uses (second-highest in the deck) and 1,390 trigger fires, the highest trigger count in the list. Kumacy is three things: bulk 2000 counter from hand, the best card to reveal when your life cracks (the trigger plays a cost-4-or-less Thriller Bark body from trash, rested), and the ideal payload for Gecko Moria or Kouzuki Hiyori to stack onto life on purpose. Treat every copy as defense or life ammunition, never as a 1-drop.

Dr. Hogback

Dr. Hogback is K.O. insurance on a body: when he is removed, his On K.O. plays any cost-4-or-less Character with a [Trigger] — other than another Dr. Hogback — from your trash, so attacking him down hands you a Perona, Baby 5, or Kikunojo on the spot. Three-quarters of his roughly 390 deploys land turns 2-3 (the going-second 4-DON opener), but he mostly lives in your hand: 2,178 recorded 1000-counter uses and 1,329 buff pitches, #4 in the corpus. His own trigger fired 1,002 times. When boarded he swings a naked 5000 over half the time — he exists to trade and rebuild, not to win races. 4 copies, mostly as resources; board him early mainly going second.

Marshall D. Teach

The OP16 addition the field adopted at 81.4% of lists (modal 2): an 8-cost 10000 whose On Play looks at the top 3 of your deck and stacks the best one face-down onto life — life gain with selection, unlike Roronoa Zoro's blind flip. The trigger is the single biggest swing in the deck: strip one character of all effects for the rest of the game, then K.O. a cost-5-or-less. Observed volume is thin — 49 recorded deploys, 82% of them on turns 4-5, and 14 trigger fires — so treat the usage picture as directional. ⚠️ no counter, so he is a dead defensive draw except as buff fodder — and none of the five highest-WR pilot pools contained him (see the flex section).

Roronoa Zoro (OP15-113)

The on-curve life builder and the deck's signature turn-2 play: turn 2 is his single biggest deploy turn — 847 of 3,053 recorded deploys, about 28%, with another 15% on turn 3 and a clear second wave on turns 5-6 (507 and 393) when lists rebuild life mid-game. Trash 1 from hand, stack the top of your deck onto life: +1 life, a freed hand slot toward the leader-draw ceiling of 7, and trash fuel if you pitch a Thriller Bark body for Gecko Moria to reanimate later. A counterless 6000 that swung at 6000-7000 in 87% of his recorded attacks. 2 copies: gold on turn 2, useful filler after.

Baby 5 (112)

Baby 5 is a 2000 counter wearing a character frame: about 20 recorded deploys against 2,033 recorded counter uses, plus a trigger — draw 2 if your leader is multicolored, which BY Nami always satisfies — that fired 642 times. She is also a premium card to tuck on top of life with Kouzuki Hiyori: a known draw-2 the opponent has to detonate themselves. 2 copies: pure defense and life payload; never spend 4 DON on the vanilla 5000 body.

Marco (Alternate Art)

Marco is the early blocker that punishes aggression: half of his 1,238 recorded deploys land on turns 2-3, bridging the gap before Borsalino comes online on turns 5-8. A 4-cost 6000 [Blocker] whose On K.O. draws you 2 cards, so the opponent either ignores him (you keep the wall) or feeds your hand by killing him. No counter, which makes him a dead late draw, and he competes with the Thriller Bark package for 4-cost board time — that is why he sits at 71% adoption and modal 2 rather than 4, and why two of the five highest-WR pilot pools skipped him entirely.

Kikunojo (Reprint)

Kikunojo is the #1 buff-trash in the entire corpus — 1,709 pitches into the leader's +2000 — and that is the job description, not an insult: counterless, so her worst case from hand is still 2000 power of once-per-turn defense. When boarded — 77% of 640 recorded deploys on turns 2-3, mostly the going-second 4-DON opener — she is a 6000 attacker (recorded swings cluster at 6000-7000) whose On K.O. refunds a life card from your deck once the opponent is at 3 or less life; her trigger self-deploys under the same condition and fired 663 times. 3 copies: early beater going second, leader ammunition in every other game.

Mr. 3 (Galdino)

Mr. 3 is the field's other OP16 experiment (53.4% adoption, modal 3): a 4-cost 5000 you park on the board, then cash in on a later main phase for draw 2 plus an attack-freeze on anything up to cost 9 — a Perona that hits big bodies and replaces itself. The observed sample is very thin — 18 recorded deploys and 11 counter uses — so the corpus cannot yet judge the slot; what it can say is that none of the five highest-WR pilot pools contained him. Treat him as a meta call against big-attacker midrange, not a default inclusion.

Gravity Blade Raging Tiger (Reprint)

Gravity Blade Raging Tiger is the only event in the consensus pool (48.8% of lists, modal 2): bottom-deck up to two cost-6-or-less characters — mass tempo that dodges On K.O. clauses entirely, which matters in the mirror, where bottom-decking Marco or Dr. Hogback denies their death value (cost-7 Nico Robin sits outside its range). Main-phase casts are not captured in this packet's usage fields and the trigger shows only 5 fires, so the slot is argued from mechanics, not volume. The real cost is the curve: 7 DON is Nico Robin's turn, and no top-five pilot pool showed it.

Girl (OP14 Release Event)

Girl is the most polarizing slot in the deck and the strongest pilot signal in the data: 48.7% field adoption, modal copies 4 — yet every one of the five highest-WR pilot pools contained her. Three-quarters of her 1,781 recorded deploys land on turns 1-2: On Play draw 1, trash 1 smooths the opener and loads the trash for Gecko Moria; then her once-per-turn Activate Main moves a rested DON onto a [Nami] card — in practice the leader, who swings 1000 higher that turn and, because the DON stays attached until your next refresh, defends 1000 higher on the way back. Add 1,703 recorded 1000-counter uses and she is never dead. Run 4 or run 0 — the data sides with 4.

Sanji (OP15-047)

The 1-of closer tech (40.9% of lists): 82% of Sanji's 266 recorded deploys land turns 6-9, which tells you the job — On Play gives one of your characters [Unblockable], so Edward Newgate at 12000 or Gecko Moria at 10000 walks past every blocker on the lethal turn. The 4000 [Blocker] body and 1000 counter (747 recorded uses) keep him from being dead earlier. Exactly 1: there are no tutors, you draw him over a long game, and the effect only needs to happen once.

Kouzuki Hiyori (Alternate Art)

Kouzuki Hiyori is the life surgeon (30.9% adoption, modal 3, but present in three of the five top pilot pools): On Play, pull a card from the top or bottom of your life into hand — firing the leader draw on your turn and rescuing whichever end is blank — then tuck any card from your hand on top of life. That loop converts Kumacy or Baby 5 into a guaranteed trigger the opponent must detonate, and moves cards you need out of burst range. Nearly half her 135 recorded deploys land on turns 1-2, and the 2000 counter (468 recorded uses) on a 2-cost body means she is live in every phase of the game.

Silvers Rayleigh

Silvers Rayleigh is the top-table removal pick the field underrates: 30.4% adoption overall, yet present in four of the five highest-WR pilot pools. Once the opponent is at 3 or less life — the state your turn-3 Nami (053) strip manufactures — he K.O.s anything up to 7000 base power, a ceiling that catches most midrange boards regardless of attached DON. Turn 4 is his modal deploy (189 of about 425), his trigger repeats the K.O. (298 fires), and the 1000 counter (734 recorded uses) keeps the floor high. 2 copies if you respect the top tables — he is the direct competitor to the OP16 newcomer slots.

Flex slots & options

The consensus is unusually solved: 19 slots at 95%+ adoption (4 Nami (053), 4 Nico Robin, 4 Zeus, 4 Borsalino, 3 Edward Newgate) and 27 more between 65% and 90% (the Thriller Bark quartet Gecko Moria / Perona / Kumacy / Dr. Hogback at 4 each, plus 2 Marshall D. Teach, 2 Roronoa Zoro, 2 Baby 5, 2 Marco, 3 Kikunojo) — roughly 46 of 50 main-deck slots locked across 3,191 pooled ranked games. The last few slots are the entire argument.

The real split: OP16 newcomers vs. the old guard. The field's answer is Marshall D. Teach at 81.4% and Mr. 3 at 53.4%. The top tables answer differently — none of the five highest-WR pilot pools (74-80% WR, 25-41 games each) contained Marshall D. Teach, Mr. 3, or Gravity Blade Raging Tiger. Those pilots spend the slots on Silvers Rayleigh (four of five pools) and Kouzuki Hiyori (three of five): targeted removal and life-stack control over raw stats. ⚠️ pilot pools are reconstructed from cards seen in their games, not verified 50s, so a 1-of that never got drawn can hide — but zero sightings across five pools and 144 combined games is hard to dismiss.

Girl is binary. 48.7% adoption with modal copies 4: lists either commit to the full playset or skip her entirely, and all five top pools showed her. The playset buys consistency — turn-1 filtering, a perpetual rested-DON feed to the leader, a 1000 counter; cutting her buys a heavier 4-cost suite. The top-pilot data sides with consistency.

Blocker texture. Marco (71%, modal 2) bridges turns 2-4 before Borsalino arrives; three of the five top pools ran him, two leaned on Borsalino plus the leader's 7000 buff as the only defense. Sanji is a 40.9% one-of whose deploy profile (82% on turns 6-9) marks him as a lethal-turn enabler, not a defensive blocker — cut him only if your meta's games end before turn 6.

The remaining options. Gravity Blade Raging Tiger (48.8%, modal 2) is the mass-tempo pick against go-wide boards; it dodges On K.O. value but fights Nico Robin for the 7-DON turn and showed in zero top pools. Kouzuki Hiyori (30.9%, modal 3) is the sleeper: a 2-cost 2000-counter that fires your leader draw on demand and is the only card in the pool that can tuck any card from your hand on top of your life — Gecko Moria stacks life only from cost-4-or-less Thriller Bark trash, Marshall D. Teach only from the top 3 of the deck. Silvers Rayleigh (30.4%, modal 2) is the top-table consensus the broader field has not caught up to.

Maindeck = 50 cards (this is the most-played legal list: 40 games, 30-10). The flex slots rotate: 4×Girl, 2×Baby 5 (112), 2×Silvers Rayleigh and 1×Sanji (OP15-047) are common swaps in/out for the 2-ofs above (Zeus 4th copy, extra Gravity Blade, or the Teach package) depending on the expected field.

What the top pilots run

The top of the Nami ladder is deep — ten pilots at 73.5% or better across 21+ games each. haru#6484 leads at 19W-3L (86.4%, median Elo floor 2421), followed by Shanwei#1765 at 19W-4L (82.6%) and Trooper#9159 at 20W-5L (80.0%). For volume, TTVISYTJJGAMER#4026 went 54W-19L (74.0%) at a 2519 floor — the largest single-pilot sample in the corpus — and sakazuki#7690 posted 31W-10L (75.6%) at 2461. IceLoom#4775 holds the highest floor (2687) at 18W-6L, while koba#5573 (16W-5L, 76.2%) and Prastik#5950 (20W-7L, 74.1%) won from floors around 1700-1900 — the winning records span the whole Elo range rather than clustering at one bracket. Rounding out the list: AKZUtaSimp#2381 at 19W-6L (76.0%) and Ninssasin#3350 at 25W-9L (73.5%).

Where reconstructed card pools exist — Trooper#9159 (80.0%, 25 games), ennenne#8446 (76.9%, 26), AKZUtaSimp#2381 (76.0%, 25), sakazuki#7690 (75.6%, 41), Prastik#5950 (74.1%, 27) — the builds converge hard. All five share the full engine: Nami (053), Nico Robin, Zeus, Borsalino, Edward Newgate, the Thriller Bark quartet of Gecko Moria / Perona / Kumacy / Dr. Hogback, plus Roronoa Zoro, Baby 5, Kikunojo, and Girl.

The disagreements are exactly the flex slots. Trooper#9159 ran the leanest package — Marco and Sanji, with no Silvers Rayleigh or Kouzuki Hiyori. AKZUtaSimp#2381 and sakazuki#7690 mirror each other: Kouzuki Hiyori + Silvers Rayleigh + Sanji, no Marco. Prastik#5950 kept Kouzuki Hiyori and Silvers Rayleigh but chose Marco over Sanji; ennenne#8446 ran Silvers Rayleigh + Sanji + Marco without Kouzuki Hiyori.

🗝️ across all five pools — 144 combined games — Marshall D. Teach, Mr. 3, and Gravity Blade Raging Tiger never appeared once, while the broader field runs the first of those at 81.4%. Pools are unions of cards seen in games, not verified 50s, so a never-drawn 1-of could hide; treat this as strong evidence rather than proof. If you are copying a list: take the consensus engine, add Silvers Rayleigh, run the full 4 Girl, and spend your own testing on the Marco / Kouzuki Hiyori / Sanji split — not on the OP16 newcomers.

The verdict triangulates: the CDN ranked aggregate (n=96) shows 28.1%, and an independent, decompile-verified 46-game replay deep-dive shows 26.1% — two sources, same story. Per-turn behavioral stats come from only 55 uploaded replays (11/12/18/14 across the four seat-result buckets) and are directional, not precise; they are labeled as such throughout.

This is Nami's worst matchup and the meta's gatekeeper: across 96 ranked CDN games she wins just 28.1% — 21.3% on the play, 37.5% on the draw — against a leader that is 29.3% of the field. The shape of the loss is precise: you put Teach at 2 or less life in roughly nine games out of ten whether you win or lose; the matchup is decided converting the last two life through a once-per-turn redirect, the 12000 blocker, and ~1.3 life of self-heal per game — while keeping your own life above 1. Take second, race to the doorstep by turn 6, hoard your 2000-counters, and unload one overloaded turn into a depleted hand. You are playing a conversion problem, not a pressure problem.

Gameplan

What Teach is. The defining grind deck of OP16: 29.3% presence at 50.6% WR across 1,865 ranked games, with a meta-warping 60.1% on the draw. Its defense is three stacked taxes. First, the leader's once-per-turn redirect — trash a [Trigger] card to retarget your attack onto any Blackbeard leader or character — which in the 46-game verified sample fired 3.1 times per game (42/46 games), 137 of 144 times onto a character: a chump like Vasco Shot eats your hit, or the 12k tanks it. Second, a body ladder: Shiryu 8000 on their turn 3-4, their 10000 Marshall on turn 4-5, Black Teach 12000 on turn 6 (18/20 of Teach's prior-corpus wins). Third, the passive +1 cost on their characters during your turn, which quietly blanks cost-capped removal. Nearly every card carries a [Trigger], so each life you crack can flip value (Van Augur -3000, Sanjuan Wolf setting their leader's base to 7000, Catarina Devon reviving fodder) and every Trigger card in hand is redirect fuel. Field corpus: Teach wins about 15% of fast 7-10-ply games (n=52) but climbs past 51% at 15+ plies (n=51). Every turn the game runs, their taxes compound.

The real problem is conversion, not pressure. In the verified 46-game sample, Nami drove Teach to 2 or less life in 92% of her wins and 91% of her losses; to 1 or less in 83% vs 71%. In 12 of 34 losses Teach hit zero life cards and still won — one logged game had Teach sitting at 0 life across six separate Nami turns. The single cleanest discriminator is your own life: average minimum of 2.33 in wins vs 1.12 in losses; Nami was killed in 0 of 12 wins and 14 of 34 losses. Getting Teach low is free. Closing through redirect + blocker + counters while staying alive is the entire game.

Your plan: sprint, steer, spike. Sprint T2-T4: in won replays winners put 90-100% of their turn-2 attacks into the leader in both seats and ~91% of turn-3 attacks on the play (n=11/12, directional), median first damage on turn 3, doorstep by ~turn 6 — and the first unredirected hit each turn also fires your leader draw (hand at 7 or fewer), so the race funds itself. Then steer T5-T7: this is the thin-sample finding that recurs in both seats — winners' share of attacks aimed at the leader fell to roughly 23-35% mid-game while losers stayed at 36-48%, and winners held incoming attacks to usually 1-2 per turn while losses on the play climbed to 2-3 by turns 5-6 (directional). Translated: winners spent the mid-game killing the ladder's attackers (Catarina Devon, a rested Shiryu, chump fodder) so the counter-war never started, then spiked one overloaded turn. Losers kept pecking the leader into an open redirect while Teach's board grew to three swings a turn and ground their hand off.

The resource war. The redirect is a constant tax, not a swing factor — Teach used it 3.42 times per game in its wins and 3.03 in its losses (flat). You do not beat it by dodging; you beat it by out-numbering answers on one turn. The number that does move: counter spend — 5.2 counter-cards per game in Nami's wins vs 6.9 in losses. Defense is the grind Teach wants you to buy. Meanwhile your draw engine (~3.8 leader draws/game, 176 events in 46 games) only pays when life actually moves — a redirected attack moves no life and draws you nothing — and 5-cost Nami's pluck (only while they hold 3+ life) advances the clock a card at a time. Their hand is the kill-timer: wins landed the final push into a median 4-card Teach hand, losses pecked into 5.

Seat: take second. The CDN split is stark — 37.5% on the draw vs 21.3% on the play (n=96) — and it compounds: Teach itself wins only 38.6% going first across 1,865 games vs 60.1% going second, so choosing second also locks Teach into its weak seat, and Nami is globally a second-seat leader (56.4% vs 51.0% across 714 games). The earlier 46-replay sample read seat-neutral (27.3% vs 25.0%), so don't rebuild your mulligan around the die roll — but the extra card is exactly the currency this matchup taxes (buff fodder, counters), and on the draw you develop on turn 1 (Girl (OP14 Release Event) on 2 DON appeared in a third of won-on-the-draw games, n=12 directional).

Honesty about the 28%. A third to half of Nami's wins coincide with Teach bricking its ladder — Shiryu appeared in only 50% of Nami's wins vs 85% of her losses, the 12k in 67% vs 82%. You can't force the brick, but you must recognize it instantly (one-character-and-pass on their turn 3-4) and convert it with maximum aggression. And do not scoop the stall: the median Teach win ends with both players at 1 life, and all nine of Nami's conceded losses were conceded by Nami — seven of them with Teach at 0-2 life. The margin is one counter, one sequence. That is exactly why play quality moves this number.

Resource control

❤️ LIFE

Your own life is the matchup's verified discriminator: average minimum 2.33 in wins vs 1.12 in losses, with Nami dead in 0 of 12 wins and 14 of 34 losses. Treat 2 as the floor you must still be standing on when the kill turn comes — not a resource to spend reaching it. Seat changes the early script: on the play, won replays kept life at 4 through turn 5 (median 4, 75th percentile 5 — they were GAINING) by buffing cheap early pokes; on the draw, winners tanked 50-58% of turn-2/3 swings down to 3 and spent cards later. Both converge on the same midgame: absorb with blockers and 1000s, never fall below 2 before your turns 6-8. Your toolkit is unusually rich: Zoro stacks +1, Robin nets +1 while firing your draw (her life-trash is a life card leaving on your turn), your Marshall stacks +1 (45.5% of won-first turn 5s), Borsalino refills at 2 or less, and Kikunojo refunds a life when he dies once Teach is at 3 or less. Their late reach — ZEHAHAHAHA and Hancock plucks, plus 2-3 swings a turn once the ladder is online — is why the losses show life collapsing to a median of 1 by turn 9 on the draw. Life management here IS board management: lost-on-the-play games faced about 3 incoming swings on turn 6, wins 1-2 (directional).

✋ HAND

Two hand rules run the matchup. First, stay at 7 or fewer cards so the leader draw is always live — it fired ~3.8 times per game (176 events in 46 games) and it triggers on ANY life movement during your turn: your attacks connecting, 5-cost Nami's pluck, Robin's self-trash, Zeus's self-pluck. Sequence those before Galdino's draw-2, not after. Second, ration counters like the game depends on it, because it does: wins spent 5.2 counter-cards per game, losses 6.9. The lost-on-the-play bucket shows the failure in miniature — turns 5-6 alone burned Zeus thirteen times and Kumacy eleven (n=18, directional); that is the alpha turn dying in defense. Trash hierarchy for the +2000 and for Girl (OP14 Release Event)/Zoro costs: counterless cards first — corpus-wide the top buff fodder is Kikunojo, spare Newgate copies, Moria, and Robin — then 1000s, and a 2000 essentially never. Watch THEIR hand harder than their life: every redirect costs them a [Trigger] card, every counter another. Wins landed the kill into a median 4-card hand (14% of the time 1 or fewer); losses pushed into 5. When Nami (053) plucks, you hand them a card — fine early (it buys life-tempo plus your draw), but it stops working once they hit 2 life anyway, so front-load it.

💠 DON!!

Pay the rent first: from turn 2 onward keep 1 DON on the leader at all times so the +2000 is live — 5000+2000=7000 walled 48.2% of their leader attacks across the sample (240/498 defended at 7000+). 5-cost Nami makes the rent free by re-attaching a rested DON on deploy, and Girl (OP14 Release Event)/Monkey D. Luffy can move rested DON after combat. On offense, size before you swing: 23% of near-lethal attacks in the prior corpus failed on raw power, and 87% of those were bare 5000-6000 swings — attach to 7000-8000 for anything that must connect. The extra 1000 to reach 8000 is Van Augur insurance: a flipped Van Augur -3000 leaves you at 5000, which still connects into their 5000 leader because ties favor the attacker. On the alpha turn Newgate is your DON engine — its on-play spreads up to 2 rested DON each onto your leader and one character, sizing two kill-turn attacks after you already spent 10. Finally, respect their 10-DON line: ZEHAHAHAHA plays the 12k from hand AND plucks your life — their turn 6 on the play. Going second, your 10-DON turn arrives before theirs: use it.

Defense guide — take, counter, or buff?

The question every defense answers: what does stopping this attack cost, and does taking it drop me below the line? Losses spent 6.9 counter-cards a game to wins' 5.2 — over-defending is the canonical way to lose.

Turns 2-3 — lone 5000-7000 leader pokes. The math: 5000 base + 2000 buff = 7000, so every 5000/6000 swing fails; their 7000 (leader + 2 DON) still connects because the defender loses ties — stopping it costs buff PLUS a 1000-counter (8000), which early is almost never worth it. Seat split from the directional replays: on the play, winners buffed essentially every early swing (100% of turn-2 swings, 77.8% turn-3, n=11) with counterless junk and kept life at 4; on the draw, winners took 50-58% and buffed just 8.3% on turn 3, banking the bigger hand. Either line is right for its seat. A 2000-counter spent here is a sequencing error, full stop.

Turns 4-5 — Shiryu 8000 and the 10k Marshall arrive; usually 1-2 swings a turn (only lost-on-the-play games exceed 2). The buff alone now stops nothing big (7000 < 8000). Default order: block the largest hit (Marco trades into draw-2; Borsalino eats a mid swing), take chips down to 3, and save the buff for their multi-attack turns — it still blanks the SMALL attacker (Devon at base, their leader) while a counter handles the big one. Won-first replays countered 37.5% of turn-4/5 swings, mostly with 1000s (Hogback, spare Nami (053)); a 2000 is acceptable only against the hit that would put you at 2 while their board is still growing.

Turns 6+ — the 12k window: firewall mode. Won-on-the-draw turn 6 is the model: winners took 0% of leader swings and countered 69.2%, with Zeus the workhorse 2000 (five logged), then the buff returned at turn 8 (83.3%) as the draw engine regenerated fodder. You are no longer defending value — you are defending a number. Count their on-board damage against your life, defend down to exactly 'alive at 2 or more,' and stack freely when it matters: 5000 + 2000 buff + 2000 counter = 9000 turns away a raw 8000 Shiryu swing; +2 more from a second counter answers 10000.

⚠️ in BOTH lost buckets the buff rate collapses to 0% by turn 6 (all fodder spent on early chips) exactly as incoming climbs to 2-3 swings per turn. If your turn-6 self-check finds no trashable junk and no 2000 in hand, the loss already happened on turns 2-4 — that is the habit to fix.

Closing the game

Count answers, not life. Zero life does not mean dead — in 12 of 34 sample losses Teach hit 0 life cards and still won, and one logged game had Teach surviving at 0 across six separate Nami turns, soaking the would-be killshot with the redirect every single time. Their answers per turn: ONE redirect (costs them a [Trigger] card), each untapped blocker, each counter card in hand, plus the occasional Sanjuan Wolf trigger making their leader base 7000. Go for the kill the turn your connecting attacks outnumber those answers — that is the whole criterion. Wins landed it into a median 4-card hand; losses pecked into 5.

Build the turn, then sequence it. Lethal math first: visible life + about 1 (they healed ~1.3 per game via Shiryu stacks and their Marshall). Then: (1) bait with the attacker you least need — if they redirect, the once-per-turn is gone; if they take it, that's damage plus your leader draw; (2) every must-connect swing at 7000-8000+, because 87% of failed near-lethals in the corpus were bare 5000-6000 swings and a flipped Van Augur -3000 must still leave you connecting; (3) Sanji makes the haymaker [Unblockable], forcing the redirect onto your biggest hit or through; (4) Newgate's on-play DON spread sizes two attackers after deployment, and Luffy has [Rush] at 6+ DON for width they didn't count. If the 12k already blocked last turn, it is rested: Newgate + 2 DON = 14000 executes it in battle before the rest of the alpha goes wide.

The window is your turns 6-8 — before or as the 12k lands (their turn 6 in 18/20 prior Teach wins, accelerated by ZEHAHAHAHA at 10 DON). Wins averaged 11.9 turns; past ~14 turns you enter the 15+-ply bucket where Teach's field WR climbs past 51%. And hold your nerve: 5-6 of the 12 sample wins ended with Teach conceding a lost board, while all nine of Nami's conceded losses were Nami scooping — seven with Teach at 0-2 life. The stall you're tempted to concede is the median win one overload turn away.

You are winning when…

  • Teach at 2 or less life by your turn 6 while you hold 3+ — in wins their life kept falling (avg 2.4 at t6 → 1.0 by t9); in losses it froze at 2.3-2.5 from t6 to t8.

  • No Shiryu by their turn 4 or no 12k by turn 6 — the brick shows in half of Nami's wins; slam life immediately.

  • Incoming attacks holding at 1-2 per turn through turn 6 (wins held there; lost-on-the-play games climbed to 2-3 by turns 5-6).

  • Two or more 2000-counters plus live buff fodder still in hand entering turn 6.

  • Teach's hand at 4 or fewer cards as they hit the 2-life doorstep (wins killed into median 4; losses into 5).

  • Game pacing toward a turn 11-12 finish — wins averaged 11.9 turns, and Teach's field win rate is ~15% in 7-10-ply games.

You are losing when…

  • Your life at 1 before you've taken a real kill turn — losses averaged a 1.12 minimum and Nami died in 14 of 34 of them.

  • The full ladder online: 8000 + 10000 + 12000 all deployed (present in 85%/94%/82% of losses respectively).

  • Facing 2-3 attacks per turn from turn 5 on (lost-on-the-play games averaged about 3 incoming swings on turn 6, directional).

  • Buff dead by turn 6 — 0% buff rate at t6 in both lost buckets because the fodder went on early chips.

  • Counter spend pacing past ~6 cards for the game (losses 6.9 vs wins 5.2), especially 2000s leaving on turns 4-5.

  • Turn 13+ with Teach above 1 life — their field WR rises past 51% at 15+ plies while yours decays with every Trigger they flip.

Top mistakes

❌

Reading 'Teach at 0-1 life' as 'almost won' and cashing attacks one at a time.

12 of 34 losses had Teach at literal zero life cards. The redirect soaks one finisher per turn forever; only an overload turn where connecting attacks outnumber answers actually ends it.

❌

Dribbling 1-2 attacks per turn into an open redirect through the midgame.

Each lone swing feeds the once-per-turn redirect at full value, moves no life (so your leader draw doesn't even fire), and lets them bank Triggers. Bank pressure, then go wide once.

❌

Spending 2000-counters on turns 4-5 chip damage.

Counter economy is the verified lever: 5.2 cards/game in wins vs 6.9 in losses, and the lost-first bucket burned Zeus x13 and Kumacy x11 across turns 5-6 alone — that is the kill turn dying in advance.

❌

Auto-firing the +2000 at every lone 5000 swing.

It costs a real card each time. Losers buffed up to 81% of turn-2 swings on the play and 91% of turn-4 swings on the draw, then had 0% buff available by turn 6; winners spent junk early (or tanked, on the draw) and still had the wall live for the firewall turns.

❌

Keeping or leaning on cost-capped removal.

Gravity Blade resolved 3 times in 46 games — the +1 tax makes it printed-5-or-less so Shiryu dodges, and Black Teach/Hancock were never reachable. Answer the ladder with the race, locks (Galdino) and blockers.

❌

Swinging bare 5000-6000 attacks on lethal turns.

23% of near-lethal attacks in the corpus failed on raw power and 87% of those were exactly these — one 1000-counter or a Van Augur trigger beats them. Size to 7000-8000 before committing.

❌

Flooding the board to 'keep up'.

Wins deployed 5.1 characters per game, losses 6.6. Extra bodies feed Devon's base-power copy and dilute the hand you need for buff, counters, and the alpha. Clean beats wide-and-broke.

❌

Conceding the 2-life stall.

All nine conceded losses in the sample were Nami conceding, seven with Teach at 0-2 life — while the median Teach win ended with BOTH players at 1. The game you're scooping is one overload turn from flipping.

Tricks & sequencing

  • Open every attack turn with the swing you least need to connect. 137 of 144 observed redirects went onto a character — once the bait eats it, the rest of your turn resolves clean; if they decline, you took a life AND your leader draw fired. Never lead with the attacker your plan depends on.

  • Sequence draws: self-life movers fire the leader draw on YOUR turn — Zeus's pluck, Hiyori's swap, Robin's trash, Robin's cycle. Resolve one of those (or land a hit) BEFORE Galdino's draw-2 so your hand is still at 7 or fewer when the life moves.

  • Tax-adjusted targeting card: Zeus KOs anything printed 4 or below (Devon at 4, Sanjuan Wolf at 4, yellow Burgess at 3, all 1-drops); Galdino locks up to printed-8 (their 10k Marshall and Shiryu, never the 9-10 costs); Nojiko bounces printed-4s INCLUDING the effect-KO-immune Burgess, because a bounce isn't a KO.

  • Kill Devon before deploying Newgate, or accept that her next attack copies 12000 base and swings 15000. If she's on board and you can't answer her, consider sequencing Robin (8000) before Newgate.

  • Sanji + your biggest body on the kill turn: [Unblockable] removes Black Teach from the answer count entirely — Teach must burn the redirect on that attack (the redirect retargets, it is not a block) or take it.

  • The 12k is mortal the turn after it blocks: it stays rested through your turn, and Newgate plus its own on-play DON spread swings 14000 — execute it in battle, then go wide at the empty wall.

  • Luffy gains [Rush] at 6+ DON on your field — deploy him ON the alpha turn for an attacker their answer-math didn't include; his reveal-pump also punishes the block if they chump with the 12k.

  • If your list runs Kid: resting him TRASHES their top life — no Trigger flips, no card to their hand, no redirect possible, no counter window, and the life movement fires your leader draw. It is the cleanest way to strip the second-to-last life before the alpha; the last point still needs a connecting attack.

Win-rate numbers are from the CDN ranked aggregate (n=96 for this matchup; Nami overall 52.0% across 714 games; Teach 50.6% across 1,865) — but the per-seat halves are ~48 games each, so 21.3%/37.5% is a strong signal with soft edges, and the earlier 46-game verified sample read seat-neutral (27.3%/25.0%). The behavioral layer is thin: 55 uploaded replays split 11/12/18/14 across seat-result buckets, so every per-turn rate quoted from them ('winners countered 69.2% at turn 6') is directional, and upload bias means those replays must never be read as a win rate. The deepest numbers (conversion-not-pressure, counter economy 5.2 vs 6.9, own-life 2.33 vs 1.12, redirect parity, the 12k's turn-6 timing) come from a decompile-verified 46-game deep-dive and replicate across its 241-game field corpus where checkable — but note its own corrections: the 'winners go wider on the kill turn' stat did NOT replicate (the overload logic stands on rules math, not stats), and Teach's self-heal is ~1.3 life/game, not higher figures you may see elsewhere. A third to half of Nami's wins coincide with Teach bricking its ladder — the plan maximizes your share of close games; it does not flip a 28% matchup. Two card-text wrinkles from the sim data: Doc Q's KO count is ambiguous between sources (1 vs 2 of your 1-cost characters), and Wyper's on-play reads as a sweep of their 2000-or-less bases (the exact wording is garbled in the sim dump) — treat both as approximate. Finally, high-WR pilot data against Teach is anecdotal (best logged: 3 games at 66.7%); nobody farms this matchup.

CDN gives Nami 54.9% over 82 ranked games -- a real but moderate sample, and the seat splits (51.2% first / 52.4% second) sit closer to even, so read 'favored, not free'. The direction is structurally credible: their consensus list runs zero life recovery and its documented staples carry zero Triggers, which is exactly the texture Nami's draw-and-heal engine farms. The replay set is only 35 games (won-second n=6, lost-second n=2), so every per-turn behavioral number below is directional.

Green/Blue Luffy is one of the ladder's most-played decks (21.8% presence, 54.5% WR across 1,386 ranked games) -- and Nami flips it to 54.9% across 82 ranked games, above her 52.0% global average. Their engine is pure tempo: the leader untaps 2 DON every main phase to fund oversized swings from 2-cost bodies like Mr. 2 Bon Clay, but the consensus list has no life recovery and its core staples carry no Triggers, so every life you strip stays stripped and every hit you take is clean card income. Take the early pokes, execute their DON carriers with Zeus, and out-resource them with leader draws plus Nico Robin life math they cannot mirror.

Gameplan

What you're up against. Monkey D. Luffy's leader text -- [Activate: Main], once per turn, untap 2 rested DON while the board is all {Impel Down} -- makes every one of their turns play like curve-plus-two. The consensus list (pooled from 5,530 ranked games) leans into it: a modal eight copies of Prisoner of Impel Down (6-cost 6000 vanilla that doubles as a 2000 counter), and full playsets of Mr. 1, Mr. 2 Bon Clay, Monkey D. Luffy, Boa Hancock, Buggy, Mr. 3, and Emporio Ivankov. Nearly every cheap body replaces itself -- Mr. 1, Bon Clay, and Buggy all draw on play; Ivankov and the 1-cost Luffy filter the top of deck -- so they never run out of gas in the conventional sense.

Their arc. Turns 2-3 are leader pokes plus Bon Clay: in won first-seat replays (n=20, directional), 71.4% of T2 incoming attacks were the leader at 5000-7000, and Bon Clay -- which copies your leader's 5000 base, then adds 1000 per stacked DON -- hit for 8000-9000 from a 2-cost. Turn 4-5 brings Buggy: draw a card, free-deploy a Prisoner with [Blocker] -- 12000 total stats plus a card for 5 DON. From T5 on, Boa Hancock takes over: 9000 [Unblockable], observed swinging up to 13000 by T6, and her On Play freezes one of your characters through your next refresh. The capstone is Let&#x27;s Go!! To The Navy Headquarters!! (94.3% of lists): rest 6 DON with five differently-named Impel Down characters and the whole board plus leader untaps for a second alpha wave. What they do NOT have matters more: no staple heals, and none of their packet-documented staples carries a [Trigger]. Their entire defense is the 1000-2000 counters in hand plus two +3000 counter events.

Your early game: take the hits. This is the loudest behavioral split in the data. In won first-seat games, Nami players took 43.9% of T3 swings and countered only 19.5%; in lost first-seat games they took 15.4% and countered 61.5%. Their early swings are 5000-7000 leader pokes -- each one you take is +1 card into hand, and the +2000 leader buff (fired on 75-85% of defended swings T2-T3 in won first-seat games) blanks the 5000-6000s for the price of a trash-fodder brick. Meanwhile your offense starts immediately: T2 winners going first put all 3 DON on Nami -- median swing 8000, 100% at their leader -- forcing a 5000-base leader to spend 4000 of counters or bleed. T3 is Nami in 55% of won first-seat games: peel a card off their life (it goes to their hand, but their staples have no Triggers to flip -- the strip costs them a life and fires your leader draw), then her rested-DON gift makes the follow-up leader swing exactly 6000, the observed median.

Your midgame: shoot the carriers. Winners pivoted hard to board control: their at-leader attack share fell from 95-100% on T2-T3 to 50.0% on T4, 46.3% on T5, and 39.5% on T6 -- roughly half of all midgame attacks went at characters. The reason is that their attackers are DON parasites. On your turn, Bon Clay is a 1000, Mr. 1 is a 2000 (his +3000 only works on their turn with 5+ hand), and Luffy is a 0 -- your 5000-6000 bodies execute them for free or tax three counter cards. Zeus headlines the purge: his KO catches everything in their consensus list except Prisoner, Brook, and Hancock, and his life-to-hand cost is a feature -- a life card removed on your turn fires the leader draw. Then Nico Robin (60% of won first-seat T5s) trashes a life -- draw fires again -- and restacks two: net +1 life and an 8000 body in one card.

The resource war. Both decks draw hard, but the shape differs: their draw is stapled to deployments (one-shot On Plays), yours is a repeating faucet -- in won first-seat games the leader draw fired 68 times across 20 games from T2-T6, call it 3-4 free cards by the time Hancock arrives, on top of your natural draws. The +2000 buff then converts your zero-counter bricks into defense: Kikunojo is the corpus' #1 trash-fodder at 1,709 logged events, with spare Edward.Newgate (1,605) and the Thriller Bark bodies (1,297-1,329 each) behind it -- and the Thriller Bark trash becomes Gecko Moria rebuy material later. Their counter wall is genuinely deep -- eight 2000-counter Prisoners plus I Know You&#x27;re Strong and Let's Go!! To The Navy Headquarters!!'s +3000 counter modes -- but every Prisoner Buggy deploys as a blocker is one fewer counter in their hand. Keep the tax on: a 7000 leader swing every turn (the won-bucket median from T4 through T8) forces 3000 of counters out of a 5000-base leader, every single turn.

Seats and proof. CDN seat splits are 51.2% first / 52.4% second (n=82) -- effectively neutral, against Nami's global second-seat lean of 56.4%. Their deck, meta-wide, is much stronger second (57.2%) than first (49.5%), so when you win the dice, taking second is doubly right: you get Nami's better half AND force them into their worse one. Going first your edge is the 5-DON T3 Nami landing before their Buggy turn; going second, winners tanked harder (took 54.5% of T4 swings, countered 9.1%) and saved the counter wall for T6, where incoming peaked at about three swings a turn. The matchup rewards reps: persuer#2839 (Elo floor ~218, 10W-4L overall) went 3-0 against this deck, and BarackPX#5464 went 2-1.
