Resource control

❤️ LIFE

Winners treat life as the cheapest currency in the matchup. The won first-seat line: median 4 through T3, 3 through T7, 2 at T8 -- they spent the first two points buying cards and then flatlined the bleed. Losers were at 2 by T4 (25th percentile: 1), and by T5 the lost-first bucket's median life WHEN taking a hit was 0 -- they were absorbing attacks they could no longer afford. The discipline stat: in won first-seat games (n=20), the median life at the moment of taking was 4 from T2 through T5 -- winners took while healthy, never while desperate. 🎯 enter T5 at 2 life minimum (3 going first), and treat 1 life as a hard floor that triggers full-counter mode. Your refill toolkit is the matchup's structural cheat: Robin converts one life into two plus a leader draw, Borsalino adds one when you're at 2 or less, Zoro restocks one for a hand card, Teach stacks one off the top three, and Moria can park a Thriller Bark body in the life pile. They have NOTHING equivalent -- no consensus staple recovers life -- so won second-seat games demonstrably healed from a median of 2 (T4-T7) back to 3 by T8. Every self-peel (Zeus, Hiyori, Robin) fires the leader draw because it happens on your turn: your life total is literally a draw engine. Theirs is just a countdown.

✋ HAND

The leader draw has a gate -- hand 7 or less -- and this matchup floods you: natural draw, leader draws (68 across 20 won first-seat games from T2-T6, so 3-4 extra by the time Hancock arrives), Girl, Whitebeard's draw-2. If you're sitting at 8 when your turn's life removal happens, the draw whiffs -- spend down. The spend valve is the +2000 buff, fired on 75-93% of defended swings in won first-seat games (n=20): trash order is Kikunojo first (zero counter value -- the corpus' #1 buff fodder at 1,709 events), stranded bombs second (Edward.Newgate (SP) at 1,605), then Hogback/Perona (1,297-1,329) which convert into Moria rebuys later -- trashing Thriller Bark is deferred tempo, not loss. What you HOLD: the 2000s. Kumacy and Zeus were top-logged counters in five of eight turn buckets of won games -- the last Zeus is often better as a 2000 counter than as removal. Keep two cards minimum entering their turn (one brick for the buff, one real counter): the lost-first bucket's T7 shows what empty looks like -- the buff fired on only 25% of swings and 75% got taken at 1 life. Their hand matters too: Mr. 1 needs 5+ cards to swing big, so every counter you force is also power off the board.

💠 DON!!

You will not win the DON war -- their leader untaps 2 every main phase, so at every turn count they play 2 rich: a second-seat T2 (4 DON) can deploy Mr. 1 plus Bon Clay and still stack a 7000 swing; their T4 (8 effective 10) is Buggy plus Prisoner plus full attacks. Stop competing on deployment and convert DON into leader attachment instead: winners' swing medians were 8000 on T2 (all 3 DON), 6000 on T3 (the Nami turn -- her rested-DON gift attaches value AFTER you spent the whole pool), and a flat 7000 from T4 through T8. The rested-DON givers -- EB03-053, Girl, Whitebeard's double gift -- are your version of ramp: post-spend attachments their math never expects. Budget removal turns so the leader still swings: Zeus plus attach on 5-7 DON keeps the 3000-counter tax running. Track THEIR DON for one tell: Let's Go!! To The Navy Headquarters!! is 1 to play plus rest 6 more (a 7-DON commitment -- their leader's untap-2 helps them reach it, but the total must still be 7+), so a turn where they sit on 7+ unattached DON with five names on board is the alpha-strike tell -- and the silver lining is that a 7-DON commitment means the second wave swings mostly at bare 5000-6000, exactly the bracket your turn-long +2000 buff blanks wholesale.

Defense guide — take, counter, or buff?

The one rule that pays for the chapter: the +2000 buff lasts the whole turn, not one battle. The leader text reads 'gains +2000 power during this turn' -- fire it on their FIRST attack declaration (you may trash even on a hit you intend to take) and Nami defends at 7000 for every subsequent swing that turn. Won first-seat games (n=20) fired it on 75-93% of defended swings every turn from T2 to T8 (peak 92.7% at T5); it is not optional tech, it is the engine. One brick stops an entire turn of 5000-6000 spam.

The math ladder vs their observed swing sizes (attacker wins ties, so you need to EXCEED):

  • 5000-6000 (bare leader, leader+1, Mr. 1+1): buff alone -- 5000+2000 = 7000, they whiff. Zero counters spent.
  • 7000 (leader+2, Prisoner+1): 7000 vs 7000 still hits -- add any 1000 counter (Perona, Hogback, Borsalino) for 8000. One real card.
  • 8000 (Bon Clay+3, Buggy+2): buff + one 2000 (Kumacy, Zeus, Hiyori, Baby 5) = 9000. The buff's value: the second card can be a counterless brick you trashed, not counter stock.
  • 9000 (Hancock, Bon Clay+4): buff + 2000 + 1000 = 10000 -- three cards for one attack. Usually wrong before lethal range.
  • 11000-13000 (stacked Hancock, late leader): take it or have pre-locked with Mr. 3. Never pay four cards.

T2-T3 -- take. Won first-seat games took 32.1% (T2) and 43.9% (T3) of swings and countered just 25.0% and 19.5%; the lost bucket countered 61.5% on T3 and died with median life 2 by T4 anyway. Early swings are 5000-7000: each take is +1 card, and you're still at median life 4 through T3 in won first-seat games. Counter only when the buff makes it free-ish (buff + 1000 vs their 7000).

T4-T5 -- pivot by seat. First seat: counter rate spiked to 48.8% on T4 (took only 24.4%) -- their swings now carry real DON and your hand is stocked from the early takes. Second seat: winners kept tanking T4 (took 54.5%, countered 9.1%, buffed 90.9%) and held the wall for T6. Either way, do not enter T5 below 2 life -- the lost-first bucket's 25th percentile at T5 was 0.

T6+ -- the Hancock era. Incoming peaks at nearly three swings a game (T5 first seat; T6 second seat, where 47.4% got countered). Blockers finally appear in the data -- 11.6% of swings blocked at T6, 16.7% at T8 -- Marco and Borsalino eat leader and Prisoner swings, but assign nothing to Hancock (unblockable) and watch Monkey.D.Luffy rest a blocker on declaration. Take Hancock at 3+ life, counter her at 2, and never face her at 1 without the Mr. 3 lock already used. ⚠️ the won-second T7 bucket took 50% of swings at median life 2 and survived because Robin/Borsalino/Teach had rebuilt the buffer -- the take-vs-counter call late is a function of your refill cards in hand, not just the number on the dial.

Closing the game

🎯 their life at 2 by the end of your T5, yours at 2+ with a refill card spent or in hand. The kill itself is a counter-math problem: their 5000-base leader needs 3000 of counters against every 7000 leader swing and 6000 -- three Prisoners -- against every 10000 bomb swing. Stack three attacks (Nami at 7000, Robin 8000, Moria/Teach 10000) and you demand 13000 of counter power per turn at 2 life; the consensus list folds inside two turns of that. Nami's peel is the cleanest point of damage in the run-up -- it never enters combat, so no Prisoner, no I Know You're Strong... So I'll Go All Out from the Very Start!!! +3000, no blocker ever interacts with it.

What they hold for the stand: eight modal 2000-counter Prisoners, Jinbe 2000s, and two +3000 leader counters (I Know You're Strong... So I'll Go All Out from the Very Start!!! and Let's Go!! To The Navy Headquarters!!'s counter mode) -- so budget lethal swings 3000 over the line, and prefer three medium attacks over one giant one. Their blockers -- Crocodile (82.1% of lists, x4) and any Buggy'd Prisoner -- each eat a swing: clear the lane first with Gravity Blade (both are cost 6 or less) or hand one attacker Sanji's unblockable (40.9% of lists run the single copy; it's worth holding all game for this turn). Expect their Mr. 3 to attack-lock your best 8-cost the turn before -- lead with Whitebeard (cost 10 beats his 9-or-less cap) or present one more attacker than you need.

⚠️ do not half-commit. Dropping them to 1-2 with a thin board while they sit on five names and 7+ DON invites the Let's Go!! To The Navy Headquarters!! untap alpha straight back into your 2 life. Winners closed through roughly one incoming swing a turn on T7-T8 because the midgame board-culling had already happened -- the kill turn is safe precisely because Bon Clay and Mr. 1 died on T4-T6. Sequence the last turn: peel first (Nami (053) or Zeus thresholds), Rayleigh's KO goes live at their 3 life, then attack smallest-to-biggest so their cheap counters are spent before the swing that matters.

You are winning when…

  • You're at 3-4 life entering T4 with 6+ cards in hand -- the won-first medians (life 4 through T3) with the early takes banked.

  • The leader draw has fired every turn since T2 (won first-seat games averaged 3-4 extra draws by T6); you're trashing bricks to the buff, not counters.

  • Their DON carriers keep dying on your turn -- Bon Clay and Mr. 1 never survive to untap, and roughly half your T4-T6 attacks are going at the board, like winners' 50-60% splits.

  • Robin resolved on T4-T5 and your life ticked UP -- the won-second buckets rebuilt from 2 to 3 by T8 while their total only fell.

  • They're at 3 or less life by your T5 with Moria or Teach in hand and Rayleigh's KO live.

  • They're deploying Prisoners as Buggy blockers -- every wall on board is a 2000 counter that left their hand.

You are losing when…

  • You're at 2 life by T4 -- the lost-first median, with the 25th percentile at 1. The game ends on their T6 Hancock turn from there.

  • You countered most of the T2-T3 pokes (losers: 61.5% at T3) and your hand is under 5 entering T4 -- now THEIR counter wall outlasts yours.

  • Hancock resolved and rested your best body with no Mr. 3 or 2000s in reserve.

  • You're taking hits at 0-1 life -- the lost-first bucket's median life-when-taking was 0 by T5 and 1 by T7.

  • Their board is five different names with 7+ unattached DON: the Let's Go!! To The Navy Headquarters!! alpha window (1 to play, rest 6 more) is open and your board can't trade into it.

  • Your buff rate is collapsing because the hand is empty -- in lost-first T7s the buff fired on 25% of swings and 75% were simply taken.

Top mistakes

❌

Counter-walling the T2-T3 leader pokes.

The data's loudest split: losers countered 61.5% of T3 swings, winners 19.5%. Those swings are 5000-7000 -- the take is +1 card, the counter is -1 to -2, and the cards you burn are the T5-T6 wall you'll die without.

❌

Saving the +2000 buff 'for a big one'.

It lasts the whole turn and is once per turn -- fired on the first declaration it blankets every 5000-6000 follow-up. Won first-seat games (n=20) used it on 75-93% of defended swings; the trash cost is a brick like Kikunojo, not a real card.

❌

Tunneling every attack at their leader past T3.

Winners cut their at-leader share to 39-50% on T4-T6. Bon Clay is a 1000 and Mr. 1 a 2000 on your turn -- leaving them up donates 8000-9000 swings every turn they untap.

❌

Paying three cards to stop Hancock at healthy life.

Buff + 2000 + 1000 = 10000 against her 9000. At 3 life you take it, bank the card, and answer with Mr. 3's lock or a Robin refill -- three cards is nearly half your counter wall for one of her many swings.

❌

Sequencing Nami after your attacks.

Her peel needs them at 3+ life -- attack first and you can lock yourself out. Correct order: peel, leader draw, THEN swing; the peel also flips Rayleigh and Kikunojo thresholds live mid-turn.

❌

Trashing 2000-counters to the buff.

Kumacy and Zeus were the most-logged counters in won games -- they ARE the wall against the 8000 bracket. Burn Kikunojo (no counter number), stranded bombs, and Thriller Bark bodies that Moria buys back.

❌

Building the defense around blockers.

Hancock is unblockable, Monkey.D.Luffy rests a blocker on declaration, and blocks only reached 11.6-16.7% of swings even in late-game won buckets. Blockers are a supplement here, never the plan.

❌

Racing to 1-2 of their life with a thin board and full DON on their side.

That's the Let's Go!! To The Navy Headquarters!! alpha window -- five names plus 6 rested DON untaps their whole board AND leader for a second wave into your low life. Cull names first or hold the wall for the swing-back.

Tricks & sequencing

  • Fire the +2000 buff on their FIRST attack of the turn even when you're taking that hit -- it reads 'during this turn', so Nami defends at 7000 against everything after, and their bare-leader and 1-DON swings (the most common attacks in the data) all whiff.

  • Zeus's cost is a feature: life-to-hand on YOUR turn fires the leader draw -- net two cards into hand before the KO resolves. Aim him at Bon Clay every time; the draw it got on play is sunk, the 8000-9000 swings it would make are not.

  • Hiyori rigs your life: take the life card to hand (leader draw fires), then plant Baby 5 -- their relentless face attacks now flip a draw-2, and with Kumacy planted they flip a free Thriller Bark body instead.

  • Sequence on your big turns: Nami peel FIRST -- it pushes them to 3 life and turns on Rayleigh's KO (Prisoners and Buggy are 6000 base, in range) in the same main phase.

  • Trash Perona and Hogback to the buff guilt-free: Moria replays them from trash on T6+, and the rebought Perona re-locks a Buggy or Prisoner on arrival. Your defense becomes future tempo.

  • Their Mr. 3 locks attackers of cost 9 or less -- Whitebeard at cost 10 is immune. When you smell the pre-lethal lock, deploy Whitebeard first and let Moria/Teach be the decoys.

  • Use your own Mr. 3 at the END of your main phase before Hancock's expected turn: draw 2 is card-neutral and the 9-or-less lock removes her 9000+ unblockable swing from a turn that otherwise brings three attacks.

  • Count their Prisoners before the kill: modal 8 copies at 2000 counter each, plus two +3000 leader events. Budget each lethal swing 3000 over, attack smallest-first to drain the 2000s, and save Sanji's unblockable for the Crocodile wall.

The direction is corroborated three ways, though: Black Yamato is a 45.8%-on-the-play deck across 1,242 ranked games, Nami is a 56.4%-on-the-draw leader overall, and the corpus' two best Nami pilots went 4-0 (Yums#2948) and 3-1 (BarackPX#5464) into this matchup.

Your best matchup on the ladder: 64.9% across 77 CDN ranked games — with an unusually wide seat split, ~51% on the play vs 77.3% on the draw. Black Yamato needs turns 1-3 to stock its trash before the 8000 Rush turns start, and a second-seat Nami reaches Nico Robin on T4 and Edward.Newgate on T5 — landing the heal-and-wall package a full DON cycle before their crest instead of into it. Take second if you win the roll; on the play, treat it as a coin-flip grind and start defending a turn earlier.

Gameplan

Their plan. Black Yamato is a trash-recursion Rush engine: any {Wano Country} character played from the trash gains Rush from the leader. The shell — Nami, Kin&#x27;emon, Yamato (098), Nico Robin — spends turns 1-3 digging and stocking the trash; the payoff is Yamato (098) trashing itself, at zero DON cost, to deploy Yamato (097) or Yamato (096) from trash as an 8000 Rush attacker, with Kouzuki Momonosuke reviving more bodies and Yamato (097) rebuying pieces to hand. The replay curve shows the shape exactly: on T2 you face only their leader (100% of incoming in both won buckets); on the draw T3 stays leader-heavy (93.3%), but on the play Yamato (097) already shows up by T3 (33.3% of incoming swings, at 8000-9000); by T4 it is the most common attacker (43.9% of incoming swings in won-first games) and volume climbs to nearly 3 swings a turn by T6.

Your plan. You are a defense-and-engine deck that gets paid for surviving. Every life movement on your own turn — your attack connecting, Nami (053) plucking their life, an Nico Robin life self-trash, Zeus pulling your own life to hand — can fire the leader draw (hand 7 or less, once per turn). In won games that engine ran near-permanently: the draw fired in 14 of 18, 14 of 18, then 17 of 18 won-first games on T2, T3 and T4, and in 13 of 14 won-second games on T3. Meanwhile your life regenerates (Nico Robin nets +1, Marshall D. Teach +1, Roronoa Zoro +1) against a consensus list that runs zero trigger cards — their damage is pure math, yours is pure profit.

Why second is so strong. CDN says 51.4% on the play vs 77.3% on the draw (n=77) — far wider than Nami's overall 51.0 / 56.4 seat profile — and three forces stack to produce it. First, DON acceleration: on the draw you untap 8 DON on T4 and 10 on T5, so Nico Robin (played on T4 in 64.3% of won-second games) and Edward.Newgate (T5 in 42.9%) land a full turn-cycle before the same plays on the play (Newgate came down T6 in 33.3% of won-first games) — exactly when their pressure crests (2-3 swings a turn through T5-T7). Second, their deck hates going first: Black Yamato runs 45.8% on the play vs 53.0% on the draw across 1,242 ranked games — a mill-then-recur deck wants the extra card and the even-DON turns too, and your second seat forces them into their worst seat. Third, Nami's kit doesn't care about losing the tempo flip: the extra starting card is one more buff trash or 2000 counter, and her leader text is entirely defensive and engine-based.

The resource war. They do not grind your hand — Portgas D. Ace's K.O. rip is their only hand tax — they grind your life with recursion that never runs out of bodies while the trash is stocked. So removal CHOICE is the real war: every battle K.O. and every Zeus hit feeds the same trash that Kouzuki Momonosuke and Yamato (097) pull from. Gravity Blade bottom-decks instead — taking Yamato (098) off the board before its free conversion AND out of recursion range is the cleanest two-for-one you have. On their side the binding resource is DON: I've Come Here To Cut Those Chains! rests 6 in Main mode and the hard-cast 8-drops cost 8, so their crest turns are all-in. Absorb one crest with Edward.Newgate plus the buff and your 2000s, and the replay pattern says their output collapses — under one swing a game across T7-T8 in won-first games, and by T8 in won-second (won-second winners still faced over two swings on T7).

Stop going face in the midgame. Winners' share of attacks aimed at the enemy leader fell from 100% on T2-T3 to 45.0% on T4 and 27.9% on T5 in won-first games; won-second shows the same slide (53.8% T3, 39.4% T4). The board is where their gas lives: Yamato (098) at 5000 dies to Nami (053) at 6000, Kin&#x27;emon (6000, no counter value) dies to a 1-DON 6000 leader swing (the attacker wins the 6000 tie), and each one killed before it converts or digs is a Rush attack that never happens. One exception: do not battle Yamato (096) — its On K.O. plays a 6-cost-or-less body from trash and refunds the tempo.

Seat-specific plans. On the draw: take the early hits (won-second players took 57.1% of T2 swings — their first-seat leader leads 7000-8000, denial costs two-plus cards, and the attacker wins ties), develop a 4-cost body on T2, Nami (053) T3, Nico Robin T4, Edward.Newgate T5, and let the heal loop carry (won-second life medians: 3 on T3, back to 4 on T4, 4 again by T8). On the play you sit at 51.4% — effectively even — because Robin and Newgate arrive into the crest rather than before it: lean harder on the +2000 buff (live for 72-79% of T2-T3 swings in won-first games), spend 2000 counters a turn earlier, and use Marshall D. Teach on T5 (27.8% of won-first games) as the bridge body before the T6 Newgate.

Resource control

❤️ LIFE

Your life is the matchup currency, and it regenerates. The won-second medians tell the story: 4 after T2 (winners took 57.1% of those swings), 3 on T3, back up to 4 on T4 — Nico Robin trashes one and stacks two — then 3, 2, 2 through their crest, and back to 4 by T8 in games that ran long. Winners took damage from strength: the median life when choosing to take was 4 on T2-T3, 3 on T4, and 5 on T5 in won-second games — that T5 take is above Nami's printed 4 because the heal loop (Nico Robin, Marshall D. Teach, Roronoa Zoro) had already banked surplus. Contrast the lost-first bucket: 3 by T4, 2 through T5-T6, 1 by T7, still taking roughly half the swings the whole way down. Operating rules: free-take leader chip at 4-3 life; gate every 8000 at 2 life with buff plus a 2000; almost never take at 1 (won-first players took just 8.3% of T7 swings). Borsalino only refills at 2 or less life — a planned dip to 2 followed by Borsalino into Robin is +2 life plus a blocker wall. And remember every life card that moves on your own turn, including Zeus pulling one to hand, also fires the leader draw — even spending life here is card-positive.

✋ HAND

The leader draw is gated at 7 or less cards and once per your turn — and in won games it ran near-permanently: it fired in 14 of 18, 14 of 18, then 17 of 18 won-first games on T2, T3 and T4, and in 13 of 14 won-second games on T3. Keeping it on means two things: always have one life movement per turn (a connecting attack, an Nami (053) pluck, an Nico Robin life self-trash, a Zeus pull) and never sit at 8-plus cards. On the spend side, budget roughly one card per turn on T2-T4 (the buff trash) and two-plus per turn on T5-T7 (buff plus a 2000 counter). Trash hierarchy comes straight from the corpus — counterless cards first: Kikunojo (1,709 logged buff trashes), surplus Edward.Newgate (1,605), Gecko Moria (1,395). Never pitch Kumacy, Baby 5 or Zeus to the buff: those 2000s are the only clean answer to the 8000 swings (7000 buffed + 2000 = 9000). Their pressure on your hand is minimal — Portgas D. Ace's K.O. rip is the lone tax — but Yamato (097) keeps THEIR hand stocked, so price 1000-2000 of resistance into every kill swing you make.

💠 DON!!

Two DON jobs every turn: curve out, and end the turn with at least one DON attached to Nami — cost-area DON does not satisfy [DON!! x1], and attached DON (rested counts) is what keeps the 7000 defense live through their turn. Won games had the buff active for 79-92% of incoming swings across T5-T7 — and 100% of the few T8 swings; that is a sequencing habit, not luck. The free enablers: Girl's Activate: Main moves a rested DON to a Nami card every single turn, and Nami (053)'s On Play does the same as a rider. On the draw the curve is clean evens: 4 = Dr. Hogback or Roronoa Zoro; 6 = Nami (053) plus one attached (the 7000 T3 leader swing in the data); 8 = Nico Robin plus one; 10 = Edward.Newgate, whose own effect parks two rested DON on the leader — buff armed, and 7000 leader swings from then on. On the play you run odds, and Nami (053) eats all 5 on T3 — her DON-move IS your buff that turn, which is exactly why she is the premier keep. Their DON tell: I've Come Here To Cut Those Chains! needs 6 rested for the mill-revive — if they pass holding 6-plus untapped, play around a Rush body next turn; if they tapped out on an 8-drop, counter events are their only remaining defense.

Defense guide — take, counter, or buff?

Their T2 — leader-only chip (one swing a game). Only Black Yamato herself attacks on T2 (100% of incoming in both won buckets) at 5000-8000; the draw keeps T3 leader-heavy too (93.3% of incoming), but on the play an 8000 Yamato (097) joins as early as T3 (33.3% of won-first T3 swings). The math: 5000 base + 2000 buff = 7000, so their 0-1 DON swings (5000/6000) bounce off a one-card investment — but a 2-DON 7000 ties your 7000 and the attacker wins ties, so it connects anyway. That tie rule creates the seat fork. Going first, their second-seat leader mostly swings 5000-7000: won-first players armed the buff for 72.2% (T2) and 78.8% (T3) of swings and took only 22-30%. Going second, their first-seat leader leads 7000-8000, where denial costs buff-plus-1000 or two counters — so won-second players simply took 57.1% of T2 swings at full life and banked the cards.

T4-T6 — the crest (usually 2-3 swings a turn at 8000-9000). Yamato (097) becomes the headline attacker (43.9% of T4 swings in won-first games) with Yamato (096) behind it. Stopping 8000 needs 9000 = buff + one 2000 — and the logged counters in won games are exactly Kumacy (6 uses on T5 in each won bucket), Zeus and Baby 5. A 9000 swing needs buff + 2000 + 1000: expensive, so take those at 3-4 life and gate them at 2. Won-second T5 splits: took 29.4%, countered 32.4%, buff live for 82.4% of swings — and the players who took were at a median of FIVE life. Yamato (096) is Unblockable: never build blocker math around it, pay from hand or take. Watch for Monkey D. Luffy granting Unblockable to a second attacker on all-in turns.

T7 and later — their gas-out. In won games their output collapses: under one swing a game across T7-T8 in won-first, and almost none by T8 in won-second. Winners armed the buff on 88-100% of the residual swings, blocked 15-25% with Edward.Newgate and Marco, and stopped taking almost entirely (8.3% on T7). If you reach T7 with a board and 2 life, you have already won — do not donate a late life to save a counter card.

The lost-game signature, so you recognize it live: lost-first T4 players took 80% of swings, countered 10%, and had the buff live for only 40% — the same turn in won-first games ran 56% / 29% / 51%. The buff costs one card and one attached DON; against a 2-3 swing turn, skipping it donates a full life.

Closing the game

🎯 survive the T5-T6 crest with a standing board, then multi-swing through a life stack that cannot fight back — the 5,554-game consensus Black Yamato list runs zero trigger cards, so every point of damage you deal is pure math with no blowout risk. What they DO hold: dense recycled counters (Yamato (097) literally returns cards to hand), I've Come Here To Cut Those Chains! in counter mode (+3000 — their 5000 leader defends at 8000), and Ground Death (+4000 once 10-plus trash, true from midgame on). So sequence the kill: leader (7000 with 2 DON) and Nami (053) (6000-7000) swing FIRST to drain events and cheap counters — each of those attacks dies to one card, which is the point — then Edward.Newgate last at 12000 (14000 with 2 DON), a number that needs three-plus cards to deny even after a counter event. Their blockers are 4 copies of Kouzuki Momonosuke and 2 of Shimotsuki Ushimaru in most lists: Sanji's On Play makes your final attacker Unblockable and turns all of them into blanks. The Nami (053) pluck double-dips — it shortens their effective life count AND procs your draw — but it hands them the card, so pluck freely in the early-midgame and stop once their hand is the last line of defense unless you finish that same turn. Expect to need two waves: a T5-T6 pressure turn that pulls counters, then the clean kill on T6-T7 when both their board and counter wall are spent — that is the exact window where won-game replays show their swings-per-turn falling off a cliff.

You are winning when…

  • You are on the draw — 77.3% vs 51.4% on the play (CDN, n=77); the seat itself is the biggest single edge in the matchup.

  • Nico Robin lands on T4 and your life is back to 4 — the literal won-second median line.

  • Edward.Newgate is down by T5 (draw) or T6 (play) with two DON parked on the leader.

  • The leader draw is firing nearly every turn — it fired in 14-17 of 18 won-first games each turn T2-T4, and in 13 of 14 won-second games on T3.

  • Their swing count collapses below one a turn by T7-T8 — the won-game signature of a Yamato deck out of gas.

  • Your midgame attacks are clearing Yamato (098) and Kin&#x27;emon before they convert — winners sent over half of their T4-T5 attacks at the board, not the face.

You are losing when…

  • You are taking T4 swings raw — 80% taken, 10% countered, buff live for 40% is the literal lost-first stat line.

  • Life at 2 by T5-T6 while they swing 3-4 times a turn — lost buckets faced 3-4 leader swings a turn on those turns, peaking above 4 on T6.

  • Yamato (097) attacks at 8000-plus every single turn while your board is two small bodies.

  • Your hand is stuck at 8-plus (leader draw off) or under 3 (no buff fodder and no 2000s for the 8000 swings).

  • Your removal has been Zeus and battle K.O.s all game — and Kouzuki Momonosuke keeps reviving exactly those bodies with Rush.

  • On the play with no Marshall D. Teach or Borsalino bridge: their crest arrives a full turn before your Edward.Newgate.

Top mistakes

❌

Saving the +2000 buff for a later turn that never comes.

Lost-first T4: buff live on 40% of swings, 10% countered, 80% taken. Winners on the same turn: 51% / 29% / 56%. The buff costs one card and one attached DON and blanks every swing of 6000 or less for the whole turn.

❌

Defaulting to K.O. removal against a trash-recursion deck.

Every Zeus hit and battle K.O. stocks the pile Kouzuki Momonosuke and Yamato (097) pull from. Gravity Blade's bottom-deck is the only removal that subtracts from their game instead of converting it.

❌

Zeus-ing Portgas D. Ace.

His On K.O. makes you trash 2 — your 2-cost removal plus a life pluck becomes a net card LOSS. Bottom-deck him or leave him alone.

❌

Building blocker math around stopping Yamato (096).

It is Unblockable, they run 4 copies, and battle-KOing it replays a 6-cost-or-less body from trash. Hand counters or take — blockers are for Yamato (097) and the leader.

❌

Ignoring a 'harmless' Yamato (098) on board.

Its self-trash conversion costs zero DON: the moment an 8-cost Yamato is in their trash, that 5000 body is an 8000 Rush attack waiting for their Main phase. Kill it or bottom-deck it before it transforms.

❌

Hoarding past 7 cards in hand.

The leader draw checks hand size 7 or less — at 8-plus your once-per-turn engine card simply evaporates. Dump counterless fodder into the buff: corpus-wide the most-trashed cards are exactly Kikunojo, surplus Edward.Newgate and Gecko Moria.

❌

Plucking with Nami (053) right before their last stand.

Each pluck hands them the life card as a counter. Early it is pure profit (clock plus your draw proc); late, against a player whose board is spent and whose hand is the only defense left, it can gift the exact 1000 that walls your lethal.

❌

Taking a hit at 2 life to save cards.

Won buckets show takes at median life 3-5 and almost none by T7 (8.3%); at 2 life, one Unblockable Yamato (096) plus a leader swing is lethal range and no blocker can save you.

Tricks & sequencing

  • End every turn with a DON on Nami: attached DON — rested included — is what satisfies [DON!! x1], and cost-area DON does not. Girl's Activate: Main does it for free every turn; from T5 onward the buff was live for 79-100% of incoming swings in won games because winners armed it before passing, every time.

  • Fire the leader draw EARLY in your Main phase: it procs once per turn on a life movement, so pluck with Nami (053) or self-trash with Nico Robin before declaring attacks — the drawn card can change the whole attack sequence.

  • At exactly 5 DON (play) or 6 (draw), Nami (053) is a complete turn: body, her On Play moves a rested DON to the leader (buff armed), the pluck procs your draw, and the leader still swings 6000-7000 — the exact T3 medians logged in won games.

  • Reserve Gravity Blade for Yamato (098) (and second target Portgas D. Ace): bottom-decking the converter denies a free 8000 Rush, removes a recursion body from the game, and never triggers an On K.O.

  • Cash Mr. 3 the turn before their crest: the attack-lock covers up to 9-cost — Yamato (097), Yamato (096), even Kouzuki Momonosuke — and the draw-2 is two pieces of buff fodder.

  • Kill-turn order: leader and Nami (053) first to pull I've Come Here To Cut Those Chains! (+3000) and Ground Death (+4000) — those events each stop a 6000-7000 swing for one card, so make them spend there. Edward.Newgate goes last: 12000 (14000 with 2 DON) needs three-plus cards to stop once the events are gone.

  • Save Sanji for the final swing of the game: Unblockable on your closer blanks all four Kouzuki Momonosuke and both Shimotsuki Ushimaru in one stroke — and Sanji himself is a 4000 blocker until then.

  • Gecko Moria can stack Kumacy face-up on TOP of your life: when their next attack lands, the known trigger replays a Thriller Bark body from your trash rested — their damage becomes your tempo — and if it survives to your turn, Zeus can pull it to hand and proc the leader draw.

📎

The replay sample is 40 games (18 won-first / 14 won-second / 5 lost-first / 3 lost-second): every per-turn percentage in this chapter is directional behavior from won and lost games, not a win-rate claim, and the lost-second bucket in particular is nearly anecdotal. Win rates come only from the CDN ranked aggregate, where n=77 is solid for the headline 64.9% but makes the exact 51.4 / 77.3 seat split soft — though its direction matches both leaders' global seat profiles (Nami 56.4% on the draw overall; Black Yamato 45.8% on the play across 1,242 games). This packet carries no hand-size profiles and no mulligan data, so the mulligan section is inferred from won-game deploy curves. The opponent build is the 5,554-game consensus list; flex slots (Sanji, Monkey D. Luffy, Shimotsuki Ushimaru counts) vary by pilot, and a list with more vanilla beef and fewer engine pieces will crest slightly earlier than the curves shown here.

CDN sample is 58 ranked games — enough to call the direction, and both seat subsamples also sit above 50% — but small enough for a wide interval. The 150-game replay corpus is healthy and its behavioral splits line up with the CDN story.

Nami is favored: 56.9% across 58 ranked games (CDN aggregate), above water in both seats, against a pillar of the format at 17.8% presence. The structural edge: every body in Rosinante's Law suite is named or treated as Trafalgar Law, so their leader's KO-save keeps converting their own shields into hand cards — and any shield that moves on your turn feeds Nami's draw. Win the card war: in won games the leader draw fired nearly every turn through the midgame (28 of 30 turn-3s going second), 5c Nami stole shields on curve, and Nico Robin landed on turn 4 in 57-73% of wins against 25% of lost-first games.

Gameplan

Their plan. Rosinante is a pillar of the format (17.8% presence, 53.1% across 1,131 ranked games) and heavily seat-warped: 58.8% on the play, 48.2% on the draw. The deck is Law-tribal ramp-tempo: 1c Rosinante digs for Laws, Marineford digs for Navy pieces and filters with its rest-a-Stage draw-1-trash-1, Trafalgar Law and Rosinante &amp; Law add DON as they enter, Sakazuki converts one rested DON into two active, and the leader discounts a 4-plus-cost Law by 2 every turn. The output is relentless mid-rate pressure: a leader swing every turn from T2 (100% of replays), Trafalgar Law at 7000 from T3, and from T5 onward Rosinante &amp; Law at 8000-9000 — by T7 that single card was half of everything thrown at winners going first (52.2% of incoming attacks, n=42). They defend with counter-less blocker bodies plus a dense event suite: I Love You!! (4 copies in 97% of lists), Mamaragan, Slow-Slow Beam Sword.

🗝️ The Law-save axis. Every Law they play counts as Trafalgar Law — the blockers Trafalgar Law, ST10 Law, and Rosinante &amp; Law foremost, plus non-blockers like OP16 Law — so the leader's once-per-turn KO-replacement covers all of them. Don't read that as removal being dead; read it as a tax that pays you. The save moves the top card of their life to their hand, and when it fires on YOUR turn (combat KO or Zeus), a life card has just been removed during your turn — exactly Nami's draw condition. Every KO attempt is heads-you-win: the Law dies, or they burn a shield, you draw, and your lethal count shrinks. The one removal they cannot tax is non-KO: Gravity Blade Raging Tiger bottom-decks two cost-6-or-less bodies — both premium blockers at once — with no save, no triggers, no recursion.

Your plan. Curve out and never miss a draw trigger. The won-game script is mechanical: Girl on turn 1-2 (about 30%), 5c Nami on 5-6 DON (71% of won-first T3s, 63% won-second), Nico Robin on 7-8 DON (57% won-first and 73% won-second, against 25% in lost-first — the largest behavioral gap in the data), then Gecko Moria (40% of won-first T5s) and Whitebeard (roughly half of won games by T5-T6). Every curve piece doubles as an engine piece: 5c Nami steals a shield on your turn, Robin self-mills one life into two, Zeus converts your life to hand — all of it triggers the leader draw. In won games the draw fired at a 76-93% per-turn clip through the midgame; in losses it collapsed (11 of 36 lost-first games drew on T6).

The resource war. They win the DON war — you have zero ramp against their four ramp effects plus Sakazuki's untap — so stop competing on it. You win the card war: your defensive baseline is one trashed card for +2000, while their premium bodies (Rosinante &amp; Law, Sakazuki, Trafalgar Law) all print blank counter boxes, meaning every point of defense they mount comes from events and small bodies. Force that trade: your late 10000-12000 swings cost them two-plus cards each, while their 8000s cost you one trash plus at most a Kumacy. Their only direct hand attack is ST10 Law — it rips 2 cards whenever you hold 7 or more — so spend down to 6 or fewer at end of turn once they have 4-plus DON.

Where your attacks go. Won games show a clean targeting pivot: 100% of T2 attacks at their leader, 93% at T3, then 46% by T4 and roughly a third from T5 onward — winners spent the midgame killing Trafalgar Law and Rosinante &amp; Law instead of racing. The reasons compound: living blockers blank your lethal turns; attacking them either clears the wall or forces the leader save (a shield off their stack plus a draw for you); and chip damage they do take converts directly into more draws. Race only when you are clearly ahead on shields or their board is locked under Perona and Mr. 3.

Seats. Ladder-wide, Rosinante is ten points better on the play (58.8 vs 48.2 across 1,131 games); Nami is the mirror image, stronger on the draw (56.4% second vs 51.0% first across 714 games). In this pairing the CDN subsamples put Nami above water in both chairs — 60.9% first, 59.1% second within n=58, directional rather than gospel. Practically: on the play your 5-DON 5c Nami turn lands before their Rosinante &amp; Law turn and you dictate the early steal; on the draw you absorb more chip (won-second players took over half of T3 swings at median 4 life) but reach 10 DON on turn 5 — 47% of won-second games dropped Whitebeard a full turn before won-first games managed it.

Answer:

Gravity Blade Raging Tiger bottom-decks it (cost 6) — not a KO, so the leader save never applies. Perona attack-locks it for a full cycle. On defense, buff plus any 2000 counter = 9000 stops the naked 8000; let the 9000 version through unless the life is decisive.

Always on — budget for the save on every KO line you take.

Answer:

Make them pay it on your turn: each save thins a shield and triggers your leader draw if your hand is 7 or less. Present two KOs in one turn (attack into Zeus) to beat the once-per-turn limit, and use Gravity Blade Raging Tiger when the body must actually disappear.

Resource control

❤️ LIFE

Your life is a battery; theirs is a countdown you accelerate. Winners going first barely touched the battery early — median 4 life through T4 and 3 through T8 (n=42) — while lost-first games sat at 3 by T4 and 2 from T6 onward (n=36). Going second you bleed faster by design: won-second medians dipped to 3 on T3 and 2 at T5, then recovered to 3 by T6 (n=30) as Nico Robin, Zoro and Borsalino (heals when you are at 2 or less) rebuilt the stack. That recovery loop is why taking early chip is correct: every shield taken is a card in hand, and every shield re-added later is bought with a card the leader drew for free. The discipline points: do not fall to 2 before your heal turns arrive (your 7-8 DON window), and treat Robin as card-neutral-or-better even when the life math looks even — her trash-then-add-two is also a draw trigger. On their side of the table, Koby pre-stacks a known shield and their own leader save eats life from the top: by the endgame they are often a shield lighter than the damage you actually dealt, and once they reach 1-2 life they can no longer afford to save Laws — your removal starts sticking exactly when the board matters most.

✋ HAND

Nami's draw needs two things: a life card moving on your turn, and 7 or fewer cards in hand when it fires. Winners kept both true relentlessly — the draw fired in 37 of 42 won-first games on T2, 28 of 30 won-second games on T3, and held near 90% going second through T5 (27 of 30), while lost-second games managed only 24 of 42 there. The failure mode is defensive hand-bleed: lost-second players used the +2000 on 79% of their defended T2s (winners 57%) while taking only 17% of those swings (winners 37%) — they paid cards for life they could afford to lose, then had nothing left for T5-T6, where countering actually decides games. Trash priority for the buff, per the corpus-wide fodder counts: spare Kikunojo and redundant Dr. Hogback/Perona because your cost-4 reanimation loops can bring them back, and excess copies of Whitebeard and Gecko Moria because they are pure redundancy — at cost 10 and 8 they can never return from the trash. Two matchup-specific hand rules: end turns at 6 or fewer once they hold 4-plus DON, because ST10 Law (modal 3 copies, in 96.5% of lists) rips 2 cards from any hand of 7-plus; and remember the draw checks hand size at trigger time, so counters spent on their turn re-open the trigger for your next one.

💠 DON!!

You will be behind on DON all game — accept it. Their ramp (Trafalgar Law and Rosinante &amp; Law on play, OP16 Law's untap, Sakazuki's rest-one-untap-two) plus event churn (Mamaragan, Gum-Gum Lightning) means they out-spend you from T3 onward. Your DON economics run on attachments instead: 5c Nami gifts a rested DON on play — the reason won-game T3 swings still hit 6000 first and 7000 second after emptying the pool — Girl repeats that gift every turn she survives, and Whitebeard hands out four at once, two to the leader and two to a body. The standing rule: bank one DON for the leader buff every time you pass. At 5000+2000=7000 it blanks every naked 5000-6000 swing they make, and won-game players used it on roughly 30-87% of their defended turns, peaking at 87% on defended T7s going first. Know the ceiling, though: attached DON only add power during your own turn, so no amount of investment defends Nami above 7000 — past that it is counters and blockers. The one DON-hungry sorcery you hold is Gravity Blade Raging Tiger at 7: on the turn you cast it, swing with what is cheap first, because the exile IS that turn's tempo.

Defense guide — take, counter, or buff?

The buff is your cheapest defense, and winners leaned on it hard — the +2000 was used on 64% of defended turn-2s, 76% of turn-3s, 82% of turn-5s and 87% of turn-7s in won-first games (n=42). It costs one trashed card and a banked DON; everything else costs more.

T2-T3 — leader chip (5000-7000 swings). Every replay opens with their leader at yours — 100% of T2 incoming, at 5000-7000 depending on attached DON. The math: buff to 7000 blanks 5000 and 6000 outright. Their 7000 two-DON swing ties you, and ⚠️ ties go to the attacker — 7000 into 7000 connects, so either add any 1000 counter (8000) or just take it. Taking is usually right at full life: won-second players took 54.8% of T3 swings at median 4 life and won anyway, while lost-second players took only 16.7% of T2 swings, buffed 79% of those turns, and bled the hand that was supposed to win T5-T6.

T4-T6 — the Rosinante &amp; Law wall (8000-9000, plus Trafalgar Law at 7000). Expect one to two attacks at your leader per turn in games you are winning, two to three in games you are losing (lost-first T6 peaked near two and a half). Priorities: stop 7000s cheap (buff + 1000 = 8000), stop the naked 8000 with buff + 2000 = 9000 exactly, and let 9000s through — buff + 2000 + 1000 is a three-card toll you should pay only at decisive life. This is the counter window: winners going second countered 49% of T5 swings versus 40% in losses; going first, 36% versus 29%. Kumacy, Zeus and Baby 5 are your 2000s of choice because all three have second lives.

T7 onward — block-and-buff endgame. Blockers carry the late game: going second, won-game blocked rates climbed from about 16% of incoming attacks at T6 to 31% at T9, while going first they peaked around 22% at T8 — on the backs of Whitebeard (a 12000 wall they cannot out-muscle without Sakazuki's help), Marco (trades into draw 2), and Borsalino (arrives with a shield attached at low life). Buff usage peaks here — 87% of defended turn-7s in won-first games — because at 2-3 life every swing is real. Final note on the engine: a counter-heavy defense shrinks your hand, which keeps the leader draw live on your next turn. Spending cards on their turn is half the reason winners kept drawing.

Closing the game

🎯 convert card advantage into one or two overwhelming turns around T6-T8, not a long chip race — their recovery suite punishes slow kills. The setup has three parts. First, shrink their stack early: 5c Nami's steal plus every saved Law is a shield that never has to be attacked through. Second, disarm the wall: Perona locks both Trafalgar Law and Rosinante &amp; Law (cost 6 or less), Mr. 3 locks anything up to cost 9 including Sakazuki, Gravity Blade Raging Tiger exiles two blockers without triggering the leader save, and Sanji makes a body unblockable if your list runs him. Third, multiply attacks: Whitebeard's gifts produce a 7000-plus leader swing alongside his own 12000 and Gecko Moria's 10000 — three attacks that each demand two-plus cards from a hand defending with 1000-2000 events, because their big bodies cannot counter from hand. What they hold against you: I Love You!! (+2000, four copies in 97% of lists, recurs a Law at 2-or-less life), Mamaragan (+1000 that replaces itself), Slow-Slow Beam Sword (+2000 and rests one of your attackers mid-turn — count it before sequencing your biggest swing last). Outs to budget for: 8c Law heals a shield and chains a body, Borsalino heals at 2-or-less life, Koby pre-stacked a known shield turns earlier. The two highest-WR Nami pilots in this dataset went a combined 5-1 against Rosinante (3-0 and 2-1) playing exactly this script: engine first, wall second, burst finish.

You are winning when…

  • Median-or-better life: 4 shields entering turn 5 on the play (won-first held 4 through T4), or a recovery back to 3 by T6 on the draw.

  • Nico Robin landed on your 7-8 DON turn — 57% and 73% of won T4s versus 25% in lost-first games.

  • The leader draw fired on at least three of your first four turns (won buckets ran 76-93% per turn through the midgame).

  • Incoming attacks held to one or two per turn through T4-T6 — their board never snowballed past your locks and exiles.

  • Their Rosinante &amp; Law is locked by Perona, bottom-decked by Gravity Blade Raging Tiger, or trading into your 10000-plus bodies.

  • Whitebeard on the table by T6 with a DON still banked for the +2000 every turn.

You are losing when…

  • Two life by turn 5-6 and one by turn 7 — the exact lost-second life curve.

  • Two to three incoming attacks per turn through T5-T7 (losses peaked near two and a half; wins stayed below two).

  • A hand bled thin by T5 after buffing nearly four of every five early swings (79% of defended T2s, vs taking only 17%) — the lost-second signature.

  • No Nico Robin by your 8-DON turn; lost-first games found her in only a quarter of turn 4s.

  • Rosinante &amp; Law swinging 8000-9000 unanswered — in lost-second games it was half of all incoming attacks by T7.

  • Your leader draws drying up: one draw across three consecutive midgame turns means you stopped attacking life and stopped self-milling.

Top mistakes

❌

Buffing away your hand on turns 2-3, especially going second.

Lost-second players used the +2000 on 79% of defended T2s and took only 17% of swings; winners took 37% and kept the cards. At 4 life a 5000-6000 hit is the cheapest thing you will ever absorb, and Nico Robin/Zoro/Borsalino refund it later.

❌

Skipping the Robin turn to make a safer-looking play.

57% and 73% of won T4s deployed Nico Robin versus 25% in lost-first — the widest win/loss gap in the replay data. She is a shield, a draw trigger, an 8000 body, and a removal tax all at once; nothing else on 7-8 DON does that.

❌

Expecting KO removal to stick on Law bodies.

Their leader replaces one Law KO per turn. Plan the sequence around it: double up KO threats in the same turn, treat a save as a paid shield plus a free draw for you, and route must-die targets through Gravity Blade Raging Tiger, which never triggers it.

❌

Tunneling every attack at their leader past T4.

Winners cut leader-targeting from 100% of T2 attacks to roughly a third by T5 — the board is the threat. An unanswered Rosinante &amp; Law swings 8000-9000 every turn while doubling as a blocker on yours.

❌

Passing with zero DON banked for the buff.

Without it their bare 6000 leader swing beats your 5000 for free. Won-first players had the buff available and used it on 65-87% of defended turns from T5 onward; that only works if a DON is committed before you pass.

❌

Counter-mathing to a tie.

The attacker wins ties. Buffing to 7000 against a 7000 swing, or reaching 9000 against 9000, is a dead defense — always finish 1000 over or take the hit.

❌

Letting the draw engine idle on quiet turns.

Turns where you neither hit their life nor move your own produce nothing. Won-first games fired the draw in 26 of 42 turn-6s; lost-first in just 11 of 36. Zeus, Hiyori and Nico Robin exist to make the trigger unconditional.

❌

Ending turns with 7-plus cards while they have ST10 Law mana up.

It rips 2 cards from a 7-plus hand for DON -1, runs in 96.5% of lists at modal 3 copies, and a 2-for-0 against the deck that wins on card advantage is self-harm. Spend to 6 or fewer — board, heals, even a loose buff — once they hold 4 DON.

Tricks & sequencing

  • Sequence 5c Nami or Zeus BEFORE your leader swing: the life movement triggers the draw immediately, and the extra card can change what you are willing to attack into.

  • Pressure their Laws on your turn even when the save is up: if they use it, a shield leaves their stack during your turn — that is a leader draw for you and one fewer card in your lethal count. Two KO threats in one turn (combat plus Zeus) beat the once-per-turn save outright.

  • Bank one DON for the buff before every pass: 5000+2000=7000 blanks their 5000 and 6000 leader swings for one trashed card. Attached DON add no power on defense, so 7000 is your ceiling — past that it is Kumacy math, not DON math.

  • Gecko Moria can place Dr. Hogback or Kumacy face-up ON your life instead of the board: when that shield cracks on their turn, the Trigger reanimates a Thriller Bark body mid-combat.

  • Perona's lock reaches cost 6 — drop her (or Moria her back) the turn Rosinante &amp; Law lands and their best attacker skips a full cycle while still costing them 6 DON.

  • Save Gravity Blade Raging Tiger for the double-blocker board: exiling Rosinante &amp; Law plus Trafalgar Law in one card is the only removal in your 50 their leader cannot tax.

  • Keep one 6000-or-less character in hand while 5c Nami is on board: if Gum-Gum Lightning or a swing KOs her, the On-KO flips a life face-up and replays the body — their removal becomes a trade-down.

  • Against Slow-Slow Beam Sword lists (about 40%), do not sequence your largest attacker last — the counter can rest one of your characters mid-battle, so lead with the swing you cannot afford to lose.

Win-rate truth here is the CDN ranked aggregate: n=58 games supports the favored call — both seat splits agree — but the true rate could sit several points either side of 56.9%. The per-seat figures (60.9% first, 59.1% second) are subsamples of those 58 and do not perfectly reconcile with the blended rate, likely due to games with unrecorded seat — treat them as no-seat-is-bad, not as precise values. The 150 replay games are upload-biased and all-Elo; they are used strictly for behavior (what winners and losers did), never for win-rate. The packet contains no hand-size profiles, no per-card win-rate deltas, and no mulligan statistics — the mulligan section is inferred from won-game deploy curves. Consensus decklists are pooled across all matchups (4,313 Rosinante-side games, 3,191 Nami-side), so copy counts reflect ladder-wide builds rather than matchup-specific tech, and Slow-Slow Beam Sword/Gum-Gum Lightning appear in only a fraction of lists. All data is OPTCGSim ranked ladder as of 2026-06-11; paper results may diverge. The high-WR pilot record (5-1 combined) is six total games — corroboration, not evidence.

The win-rate itself rests on only 38 CDN ranked games, so 47.4% reads as a true coin flip with wide error bars rather than a precise edge. Every behavioral claim, however, rests on 1,409 high-Elo uploaded replays (584 won on the play, 384 won on the draw, 145 and 296 lost) - the deepest behavioral sample in this guide.

Statistically even - 47.4% across 38 ranked games - but it never plays even: Enel runs a 6-card DON deck by rule, sprints from turn 2, and decays after turn 6. Your job is to tax the early 5000-7000 leader swings with the +2000 buff, hit the EB03 Nami turn-3 and Nico Robin turn-4/5 curve, and stretch the game - won uploads averaged 6.8-6.9 turns against 6.3 in losses. Seat matters more than usual: Nami took 50% of first-seat games but only ~43% on the draw (n=38, thin), against a leader that wins 64.6% on the play meta-wide.

Gameplan

Their plan: convert a capped DON pool into immediate stats. Enel's leader text caps their DON deck at 6 cards, and in exchange, from turn 2 they add 1 active DON plus up to 4 rested every turn, then dump up to 4 rested DON onto one character. The deck is built to spend that burst instantly: 16 slots of 0-cost DON-fueled events - Lightning Beast Kiten and Lightning Dragon (DON!!1: draw 1), Mamaragan (DON!!2: draw 1), El Thor (DON!!1: +1000 pump plus a KO on a 3000-or-less character) - plus 1-cost draw bodies (Ohm and Shura as 4-ofs in ~100% of lists, Satori in 46.6%). On their second turn the leader itself is 59-62% of all incoming attacks at 5000/7000, with Shura Rushing in at 7000-8000. From your T4 onward Enel (118) takes over: 8000 base, +2000 and effect-removal-proof while they hold 6 or less DON (always true), swinging 10000 standing and 14000 with the leader's 4-DON dump. It is 19.5-28.1% of incoming attacks T4-T6 in won games on the play, and up to 37-40% in your losses on the draw. Their attack volume peaks T4-T6 at usually two, sometimes three swings a turn.

The structural weakness: 6 DON forever. They never untap more than 6 DON, their curve tops at the 6-cost Enel (118), and every draw event competes with the pump for the same capped pool - a 14000 turn is a low-draw turn for them. The clock data shows what that means: across the uploads, won games averaged 6.75 turns on the play and 6.92 on the draw; lost games averaged 6.34 and 6.30. Roughly half a turn of extra game length separates winning from losing, because your deck keeps scaling to 9-10 DON (Gecko Moria, Edward.Newgate) while theirs flatlines.

Your plan in one line: deny cheap, curve hard, outlast. Early, the +2000 buff plus a 1000-counter beats everything they throw (in 584 wins on the play, the buff fired on 87% of T2 swings and winners took only 18.2% of them). On curve, EB03 Nami on T3 is the single biggest deploy gap in the data - 61.1% of winners' T3 deploys on the play versus 40.7% in losses - and Nico Robin owns T4 on the draw (66.7% in wins versus 47.3% in losses). Robin is the engine of the life race: trash 1 from your life (which fires your leader draw - a card left your life on your turn), add 2 back, net +1 life plus a card, plus an 8000 body that burns them for 1 when it dies on their turn. By your T6, winners on the play had Enel at about 1 life on average while sitting at 2.4 themselves.

The resource war. Their card economy is DON-1 events; yours is the leader draw, and winners kept it running: across those 584 first-seat wins the draw fired 492 times on T2, 469 on T3, 454 on T4 and 425 on T5 - over 1,800 extra cards, about three per game by the end of T5. In losses the rate decays (in 296 second-seat losses, 149 draws on T5 - roughly half a draw per game versus 0.7 in wins). Hand curves tell the same story: winners on the play held about 5 cards through T5 and 4.2 at T7; losers held 4.66 falling to 3.66, and second-seat losers collapsed to 2.5 by T9. Feed the buff with the right fodder - corpus-wide the most-trashed cards are Kikunojo, spare Edward.Newgate, Gecko Moria, Dr. Hogback and Perona - and never your 2000-counters. The cost-4 bodies (Kikunojo, Hogback, Perona) are rented, not burned - all your recursion (Moria, Hogback, the Thriller Bark triggers) caps at cost 4; the spare Newgate and Moria copies are duplicate top-end the game usually ends before you could replay.

The counter-suite asymmetry (exploit this). Their 0-cost +2000 counters - Varie, El Thor, Lightning Beast Kiten - only land on [Enel] cards: the leader, Enel (118), Enel (060). Their other bodies can only be saved by Mamaragan's +1000 or Divine Departure's +3000-for-a-trash. Winners clearly leaned into this: their share of attacks aimed at the leader fell from ~100% on T2 to 59% on T4 and 31-36% from T6 on. Mid-game, swinging into Ohm, Holly and the blockers is cheap removal their counter wall barely protects, and it strips the Double Attack closer before it matters.

Seats flip your usual preference. Nami overall wins more on the draw (56.4% versus 51.0% across 714 CDN games), but against Enel the CDN split is 50.0% on the play and 42.9% on the draw (n=38, thin but directionally consistent with Enel's meta-wide 64.6% first-seat win rate). On the play you crack their first life on T2 in 85% of eventual wins and control the tempo. On the draw, your first life falls on T2 in 44% of even the games you go on to win - you are defending from minute one, and the Nico Robin T4 stabilizer turn is the whole seat.

Their threats

Enel (OP15-058) OP15-058
Role:

The ramp engine: +1 active and 4 rested DON per turn from T2, with a 4-DON dump onto one character. The leader itself is your biggest early attacker - 59-62% of T2 incoming swings at 5000/7000.

When:

Every turn from their second.

Answer:

Tax it. Buff to 7000 stops the naked 5000; buff plus any 1000-counter (8000) stops the 7000. Every denied swing wastes a turn of a DON pool that is capped at 6 by rule.

Enel (OP15-118) OP15-118
Role:

Primary beater: 10000 standing (8000 base +2000 while they have 6 or less DON - always), 14000 with the leader's 4-DON dump, and immune to effect removal in the same condition. On Play digs 5 deep.

When:

From your T4: 19.5-28.1% of incoming attacks T4-T6 in wins on the play, 37-40% T5-T7 in losses on the draw.

Answer:

Never counter the 14000 (you would need 10000 of help on a 5000 leader). Attack-lock it with Perona or Mr. 3 (cost 6 and 9 locks both work), block with Edward.Newgate, or battle-KO it while rested: Nico Robin 8000 + 2 DON = 10000 kills it, since ties favor the attacker and immunity only covers effects.

Shura OP15-067
Role:

Rush opener - 2000 base that hits for 7000-8000 the turn it lands off the leader's DON dump.

When:

T2-T3: 10-13.5% of early incoming attacks.

Answer:

Expect one on their second turn and budget a counter or the buff for it. Afterward it is a 2000 vanilla - free food for Zeus or any swing.

Charlotte Pudding OP12-071
Role:

Their consistency: searches Sanji or any Event, then doubles as a pumped 7000-8000 attacker early.

When:

T2-T3: 13.7-28.2% of incoming attacks across buckets.

Answer:

Same math as the leader swings - buff plus 1000 stops 7000. Kill it with Zeus when convenient; every dead search body slows the event chain.

Holly OP15-071
Role:

The race-flipper: gives all their Ohm copies and itself Double Attack, and makes them 6000 base on your turn so they do not die for free.

When:

Mid-game; Ohm carries roughly 10-13% of incoming attacks T3-T8 at 2000/7000 common powers.

Answer:

⚠️ at 2 life, a 7000 Double Attack Ohm swing is the kill - that is the swing you counter, not the leader's. Proactively Zeus the Holly (cost 3) or Ohm (cost 1) before it ever attacks.

Vinsmoke Reiju OP12-063
Role:

7000-power blocker once they have 4+ events in trash, and at +5 cost (9 total) it dodges Zeus, Gravity Blade Raging Tiger and Perona.

When:

T4 onward; 9.5-13.9% of incoming attacks in your losses T5-T7 - it shows up more when you lose.

Answer:

Silvers Rayleigh KOs by base power (5000, under the 7000 line) regardless of cost, live once their life is at 3 or less. Mr. 3 attack-locks cost 9. Otherwise plan lethal through one block.

Gamma Knife (Reprint) OP05-077
Role:

-5000 to one of your characters on their main phase; 98.5% of lists run 3.

When:

Any turn they can spare the DON-return; worst on the turn they want a big body dead.

Answer:

Assume each of Nico Robin / Edward.Newgate eats one: Robin at 3000 or Newgate at 7000 dies to the next swing. Deploy redundancy - never let one body be your whole defense.

Trafalgar Law (ST10-010) (Alternate Art) ST10-010
Role:

Hand hate stapled to a blocker: if you hold 7+ cards they trash 2. In 52.9% of lists, usually 2 copies.

When:

From their 4-DON turns.

Answer:

Cap your hand at 6 when it could land. Your leader draw needs 7 or less anyway - banking to 8 turns the engine off AND exposes you to Law.

On the draw, weight Nico Robin and Zeus up: Robin is two-thirds of winners' T4 deploys there, and Zeus answers their 1-cost draw bodies on T2. Multiple top-end pieces (Edward.Newgate, Gecko Moria, Marshall D. Teach) are your buff fodder, not your keeps - the games are decided by T6 and a duplicate 8-10-cost body almost never gets a turn to land.

Resource control

❤️ LIFE

Treat 2 life as the floor, not a checkpoint on the way down. Winners on the play averaged 3.37 / 2.95 / 2.61 / 2.36 life across T3-T6; losers averaged 3.15 / 2.39 / 1.82 / 1.51, and second-seat losses hit a median of 1 by T6 with a quarter of those games at 0. The half-life-per-turn gap is built from three sources: denying the cheap T2-T3 swings (winners took only 18-35% of them), Nico Robin's net +1 life on T4-T5, and Borsalino's refill that turns on at exactly 2 or less. Gecko Moria and Marshall D. Teach can also bank cards into life late. Two mechanical notes govern everything: damage you take on their turn hands you the life card but never fires the leader draw (the effect is [Your Turn] only), while life that leaves on your own turn - Robin's trash, Zeus or Kouzuki Hiyori's life-to-hand, EB03 Nami's steal of theirs - always does. So your life total is also a draw battery, but only when you spend it on your own clock. On offense, crack their first life by T2-T3 (85% of first-seat wins did it on T2) and aim them at ~1 life by your T6, which is exactly where winners' averages sat. The steal on EB03 Nami only works while they hold 3+ life - sequence her early, not as a finisher.

✋ HAND

Two hard ceilings define your hand: the leader draw requires 7 or less cards, and Trafalgar Law trashes 2 if you hold 7+ - so the correct resting state is 5-6 cards, engine on, Law blanked. Winners lived there: first-seat wins averaged 5.94 cards on T2, still 5.01 at T5 and 4.23 at T7; first-seat losses ran 4.66 at T5 down to 3.23 by T8, and second-seat losses collapsed to 2.52 by T9. The engine keeps you afloat - the draw fired about three extra cards per game through T5 in first-seat wins, and in second-seat games the T5 rate was roughly 0.7 per game in wins versus 0.5 in losses - but only if you keep attacking into life and manufacturing your-turn life movement. Spend discipline: the +2000 buff costs a trash every time, and across the whole corpus the most-trashed cards are Kikunojo, spare Edward.Newgate, Gecko Moria, Dr. Hogback and Perona. Pitching the cost-4 trigger bodies (Kikunojo, Hogback, Perona) is renting, not burning - Moria, Hogback and the Kumacy triggers all play back cost 4 or less; pitching a spare Newgate or Moria is for keeps, and still right - the game rarely lasts long enough to deploy a second one. Pitching Kumacy or Zeus to the buff is the quiet way losses happen: budget roughly two cards per defended turn through T4-T6 and make sure the 2000-counters are the last to go.

💠 DON!!

This is the only matchup axis where you are simply bigger. Their DON deck is 6 cards by rule - they never untap more than 6, and the leader's dump sends 4 of them to one character, so a 14000 Enel (118) turn leaves at most 2 DON for draw events. Every turn they choose between velocity (events) and violence (the pump); your defense quality decides how often the violence pays. You, meanwhile, climb to 9-10 DON by T5-T6 and play leader-plus-two-bodies turns they mathematically cannot fully answer. Three DON habits carry the matchup. First, end every single turn with at least 1 DON attached to Nami - the +2000 requires [DON!! x1] and attached DON persists through their turn. Winners' buff usage (540 activations on T2 alone across 584 first-seat wins) is only possible with that habit. Second, exploit the free DON economy: Girl gifts a rested DON to a [Nami] card once per turn and EB03 Nami hands one back on arrival - that is why winners still swung 6000-7000 on the turns they curved out. Third, Edward.Newgate's 2+2 rested DON arrive attack-ready: sequence him before your swings and the turn he lands is also your biggest attack turn.

Defense guide — take, counter, or buff?

Every swing costs one of three currencies - life, hand, or the once-per-turn +2000. The data says winners spend them in a specific order by phase.

Phase 1, their T2-T3 (swings at 5000-7000): deny almost everything. In 584 first-seat wins, players took only 18.2% of T2 swings, countered 40.7%, and activated the buff on 87% of them; on T3 it was 34.6% taken with the buff at 69.2%. The math is why: bare buff = 5000 + 2000 = 7000, which beats their naked 5000 leader swing outright; their 7000 (+2 DON) swing needs the buff plus any 1000 - 8000 beats 7000 (never forget ties favor the attacker: buff alone at 7000 versus 7000 still hits). Winners' actual receipts match: the top T2 counter plays were Perona and Dr. Hogback pitched at 1000 (70 and 66 uses), exactly the buff-plus-1000 line. Resist the take-early reflex you use elsewhere: damage on their turn never fires your leader draw, and each denied swing wastes a full turn of a 6-DON-capped engine. The win/loss gap here is small but real - winners countered 40.7% on T2 versus 37.4% in losses, 30.7% versus 27.0% on T3.

Phase 2, T4-T6 (the Enel (118) era): triage. The 118 is 19.5-28.1% of incoming attacks in first-seat wins at 10000/14000. A 14000 needs 10000 of help on your 5000 leader - never defend it; a 10000 needs the buff plus 4000 - usually still no. Winners' buff rate collapsed from 87% on T2 to 40.4% on T4 while losers kept buffing at 49.9% - burning hand into swings they could not flip. Taking 47.9-51.6% of swings on T5 is what WINNING looks like in this phase, not failure. Save the buff and counters for the flippable swings: the leader at 7000, Ohm at 7000, Vinsmoke Reiju at 7000. ⚠️ if Holly is on board, Ohm has Double Attack - at 2 life that 7000 swing is lethal range and it is the one attack per turn you must answer, 14000s be damned. From T6 your blockers come online (Borsalino, Marco, Edward.Newgate): blocked rates in wins rise from 0% early to 8.5-9.4% on T6, and the right block is the biggest swing you cannot counter - Newgate at 12000 even eats a 14000 as a body-for-life trade.

Phase 3, T7+ (both tanks empty): keep defending - this is where losers quit. On the play at T8, winners countered 29.2% of swings and took 43.5%; losers countered 19.6% and took 56.5%. Buff usage climbs back up (80% of T9 swings in first-seat wins; 54.8% with 19.2% blocked in second-seat wins) because winners actually have cards left - the dividend of not buffing into 14000s three turns earlier. The take-at medians tell you the line: winners took hits while at 3 life early and 2 life late. If you are taking at 1, the script has already failed - find the counter or the block.

Closing the game

🎯 their life at ~1 entering your T6 - that is exactly where first-seat winners' average sat (about 1.9 at T5, 1.1 at T6) in games averaging 6.75 turns. The kill itself is an attrition problem, not a power problem. Their leader is 5000 with no native counter bodies above 1000 - the wall is hand counters: Varie, El Thor and Lightning Beast Kiten at +2000 each (Enel cards only), Mamaragan at +1000 plus a draw, Divine Departure at +3000 for a trash. Budget as if every card in their hand is +2000: a single 10000 Nico Robin swing into the 5000 leader demands three cards; three 7000-8000 swings demand five-plus counter cards - more than their hand can keep supplying turn after turn. That is why winners' attack pattern flipped - 31-36% of attacks at the leader from T6 on, the rest into characters: strip Ohm/Holly (their counters mostly cannot protect non-Enel bodies), clear Franky, Trafalgar Law and Vinsmoke Reiju blockers, then spend the drained hand's leftovers on the buffed leader push. Two specific lethal tools: Silvers Rayleigh KOs the grown Reiju by base power once their life is 3 or less, and the 1-of Sanji (in 40.9% of lists) makes your biggest attacker unblockable so Enel (060)'s on-demand blocker cannot ambush the kill turn. Remember battle beats immunity: a rested 10000 Enel (118) dies to Robin 8000 + 2 DON (ties to the attacker) or Edward.Newgate - just expect one +2000 event in response. And do not shave your own life to 1 to race a Holly board: their Double Attack outpaces you from there. The ceiling on this matchup is high - the four highest-win-rate Nami pilots in the corpus went a combined 17-0 in uploaded games against Enel (including Pirate93136#5070 at 6-0 around 2459 Elo) - the even CDN number is an average over pilots who have not internalized the triage rules above.

You are winning when…

  • EB03 Nami hit the board on your T3 - winners did it in 61% of games in both seats; first-seat losers managed only 41%.

  • Their first life cracked on your T2 (85% of first-seat wins) or by T3 on the draw (~75% of second-seat wins).

  • You enter T5 at 3 life on the play or 2+ on the draw - winners averaged 2.6 / 2.1 there versus 1.8 / 1.5 in losses.

  • Hand still at 5 cards on T5 with the leader draw firing most turns (about three extra cards by end of T5 in first-seat wins).

  • Their attack count is sagging by T6-T7 (under two swings) while your board adds Borsalino or Edward.Newgate - the 6-DON engine is out of gas.

  • The game is heading past turn 7: won uploads averaged 6.75-6.92 turns, losses 6.30-6.34 - length is your friend.

You are losing when…

  • You are at 1 life by T6 - the second-seat loss median, with a quarter of those games already at 0.

  • Hand at 3 or less by T6-T7 while still taking half their swings - the spend-order failed somewhere around T4.

  • Enel (118) has swung 14000 on consecutive turns with no Perona, Mr. 3 or Edward.Newgate answer in sight - in losses it carried 37-40% of all incoming attacks.

  • Vinsmoke Reiju is blocking at 7000 and attacking at 7000-11000 - it features far more in your losses (9.5-13.9% of incoming T5-T7) than your wins.

  • You are pitching Kumacy and Zeus to the +2000 buff - counter quality is gone and the late-game defense rates (winners 29% countered at T8, losers 20%) follow.

  • Their swing volume is still two-and-a-half-plus per turn at T6 (the second-seat loss pattern) - you never blunted the tempo and the race is theirs.

Top mistakes

❌

Buffing the leader into 10000/14000 Enel (118) swings.

5000 + 2000 = 7000 does nothing against 10000; you trash a card for zero. Winners' buff rate fell from 87% on T2 to 40.4% on T4 exactly as the 118 arrived; losers stayed at 49.9% and bled hand.

❌

Tanking the T2-T3 leader swings out of take-early habit.

Nami's draw is [Your Turn] only - their hits never feed it. Winners took only 18.2% of T2 swings; the buff-plus-1000 denial costs two cards but wastes an entire turn of their capped 6-DON output.

❌

Skipping EB03 Nami on T3 to hold up counters.

It is the single most win-correlated play: 61.1% versus 40.7% T3 deploy rate in first-seat wins versus losses. Her DON gift means you barely lose attack power, and the steal pays you a leader draw.

❌

Slow-rolling Nico Robin past T4-T5.

The deploy gap is massive in both seats (66.7% vs 47.3% on the draw at T4; 35.4% vs 15.2% on the play). Every turn she waits, their two-to-three-swing turns eat the life she would have rebuilt.

❌

Banking to 7+ cards in hand.

The leader draw needs 7 or less to fire, and Trafalgar Law (52.9% of lists) trashes 2 on sight. Park at 5-6: engine on, Law blank.

❌

Pointing effect removal at Enel (118) or Enel (060).

Both are immune to effect removal while they have 6 or less DON - which is always, by rule. Zeus and Gravity Blade Raging Tiger literally cannot touch them; the answers are attack-locks, blocks and battle.

❌

Sending every late-game attack at the leader.

Their +2000 counter events only protect [Enel] cards, so leader swings are maximally taxed. Winners cut leader-targeting to 31-36% from T6 and killed Ohm/Holly/blockers instead - removal their counter wall cannot contest.

❌

Trashing live counters to the +2000 instead of recursion fodder.

Corpus-wide, the correct fodder is Kikunojo, spare Edward.Newgate and the Thriller Bark bodies (Dr. Hogback, Perona) that Gecko Moria and the triggers resurrect. Pitching 2000-counters is permanent; pitching trigger bodies is a loan.

Tricks & sequencing

  • End every turn with at least 1 DON attached to Nami - it persists through their turn and is the [DON!! x1] requirement for the +2000. Winners activated the buff 540 times on T2 alone across 584 first-seat wins; that only happens with this habit.

  • Zeus on your turn is a two-for-one: the life-to-hand cost is a card leaving your life on your turn, so the leader draw fires - KO their Holly or a draw body and refill in the same action.

  • Nico Robin's On Play also fires the leader draw (the trashed life card left your life on your turn): net +1 life, +1 card, 8000 body, all in one deploy.

  • EB03 Nami at exactly 5 or 6 DON still swings: she gifts a rested DON to the leader, which is why winners' T3 median swings were exactly 6000 on the play and 7000 on the draw.

  • Battle beats immunity: a rested Enel (118) at 10000 dies to Robin 8000 + 2 DON (ties favor the attacker) or Edward.Newgate's 12000 - 'cannot be removed by effects' says nothing about combat. Expect one +2000 event in defense and add 2 DON - Robin 8000 + 4 DON = 12000 ties through it; Newgate's 12000 already does.

  • Perona's On Play attack-locks the cost-6 Enel (118) for a full turn cycle, and her On K.O. does it again - she answers the unremovable threat twice and pitches at 1000 in between.

  • Mr. 3 trashes itself for draw 2 plus an attack-lock on anything cost 9 or less - the only clean answer to a grown Vinsmoke Reiju, and it works on the 118 too.

  • Aim mid-game attacks at non-Enel bodies: Varie, El Thor and Lightning Beast Kiten can only counter onto [Enel] cards, so Ohm, Holly and Charlotte Pudding can only be saved by Mamaragan's +1000 or Divine Departure's +3000.

There is no direct mulligan telemetry - keep/toss advice is inferred from winners' deploy curves. Occasional 0-power entries in the attacker power lists are parser artifacts and were ignored. The 6-DON cap is straight from Enel's printed leader text and is corroborated by observed attack powers (the 14000 Enel (118) swings are 8000 base +2000 self-buff +4000 leader dump).
